Mallory and Irvine had died on the mountain in 1924 — whether they summited remains unknown.

question: The world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 metres has a fatality rate among summit attempters of about 13% — much higher than Everest's roughly 3%. Climbers call it 'the savage mountain'. It sits in the Karakoram Range on the Pakistan-China border. What is it called?
context: K2 was first climbed by the Italian expedition of Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli in 1954. Its name comes from a 19th-century survey numbering; the K stood for Karakoram. Of 14 eight-thousanders, K2 has the highest fatality rate after Annapurna.

question: On the Tanzania-Kenya border rises the highest free-standing mountain in the world — a 5,895-metre volcano whose summit holds glaciers at the equator. The mountain has three distinct volcanic cones; the highest, Kibo, is dormant but not extinct. What are the three cones called?
context: Shira is the oldest and most eroded; Mawenzi is rugged and peaked; Kibo is the youngest and tallest. The summit glaciers — climate-changed and shrinking rapidly since the 19th century — are predicted by some scientists to disappear by mid-century.

question: The highest peak in North America rises 6,190 metres in interior Alaska. Originally known by the Koyukon Athabascan name meaning 'the high one', it was officially named Mount McKinley by Congress in 1917 over local objection, and was renamed back by federal order in 2015. What is its name today?
context: Denali is the steepest mountain on Earth from base to peak — its base sits at about 600 metres elevation, giving a vertical relief of about 5,500 metres. Everest's base camp sits at 5,300 metres, so its base-to-summit relief is only about 3,500 metres.

question: In western Argentina near the Chilean border rises the highest peak in the Western Hemisphere — and the highest mountain outside Asia — at 6,961 metres. It is unique among the world's high peaks in being climbable by a 'walk-up' route requiring no technical climbing. What is its name?
context: Aconcagua means 'sentinel of stone' in Quechua. The non-technical Normal Route on the north face still requires acclimatisation; the Polish Glacier route on the east is challenging. About 35% of attempts succeed.

question: The highest peak in Europe sits in southern Russia on the boundary between Europe and Asia — a 5,642-metre dormant volcano in the Caucasus range. Whether it counts as Europe's top depends on where Europe's boundary is drawn; under most definitions it does. What is its name?
context: Mont Blanc (4,810 m) is sometimes called Europe's highest if the Caucasus is excluded as Asian. Elbrus has two summits — both dormant volcanic peaks. The Soviets built a cable car system on the south side; Elbrus is one of the easier 'Seven Summits'.

question: The highest peak in the Alps rises 4,810 metres on the France-Italy border. It was first climbed in 1786 by Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard — a feat that launched modern mountaineering. Whose financial reward made this climb attractive?
context: Saussure, a Swiss geologist, had offered a reward to the first man to reach the top in 1760. Twenty-six years later Balmat and Paccard succeeded; Saussure himself climbed it the following year. The pioneers of Alpine climbing were as much scientists as adventurers.

question: On the Swiss-Italian border rises a 4,478-metre peak with an iconic pyramid silhouette — one of the most photographed mountains on Earth. The first ascent was a triumph and a disaster: four members of the seven-man party died on the descent when a rope broke. Who led the successful 1865 climb?
context: The seven climbed up the Hornli ridge from Zermatt on 14 July 1865 — beating an Italian team to the summit by hours. Descending, Douglas Hadow slipped; Whymper and the two Taugwalders survived because the rope between them and Hadow's group broke. The Matterhorn now sees about 3,000 ascents a year.

question: On Japan's main island of Honshu, an almost perfectly symmetrical volcanic cone rises 3,776 metres — the highest peak in Japan, last erupted in 1707-1708 (the Hoei eruption). The mountain is sacred in Shinto and is the country's most-painted, most-photographed natural symbol. What is it called?
context: Fuji is a stratovolcano formed from three overlapping volcanoes. About 300,000 people climb it during the official July-September climbing season. The Hoei eruption blew a side crater (Hoeizan) into the cone's east flank — visible from below. UNESCO World Heritage 2013 as a cultural rather than natural site.

question: In western Tibet rises a 6,638-metre mountain considered sacred by four religions — Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and the Bon — and is therefore not climbed; no one has officially summited it. Pilgrims walk a clockwise 52-km circuit at its base. What is the mountain called?
context: Hindus consider Kailash the home of Shiva. Buddhists consider it the seat of Demchok. Jains consider it where Rishabhanatha attained enlightenment. The Bon consider it the seat of their sky goddess Sipaimen. Reinhold Messner declined an offer to climb it out of religious respect.

question: Down the western coast of South America runs the longest continental mountain range on Earth, about 7,000 km from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego, passing through seven countries. The range was raised by the subduction of one ocean plate beneath the South American plate. Which subducting plate?
context: The Andes are still rising as the Nazca plate continues to subduct at about 6-7 cm per year. The range is the world's second-highest (after the Himalayas). Volcanoes line its length: Cotopaxi, Chimborazo, Aconcagua, Ojos del Salado, and many others.

question: The Himalayas — which contain all 14 of the world's mountains over 8,000 metres — were formed (and are still forming) by which tectonic event?
answer: The Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate (started ~50 million years ago)
choices: The Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate (started ~50 million years ago)
The Pacific Plate subducting beneath the Eurasian Plate
Volcanic activity along a divergent hotspot in northern India
Ancient glaciation eroding a Tibetan plateau to leave high ridges
context: The Indian plate was a separate continent attached to Antarctica until about 130 million years ago, when it broke off and drifted north at unusually high speed (15 cm per year). It collided with Asia around 50 million years ago; the leading edge of India is still being driven northward, pushing Tibet up.

question: The Karakoram Range, on the borders of Pakistan, China, and India, holds an unusually dense concentration of the world's highest peaks. Four of the fourteen 8,000-metre peaks sit in the Karakoram, in a remarkably small area. They are K2, Gasherbrum I, Gasherbrum II, and which other?
context: All four sit within a 20-km cluster around the Baltoro Glacier. The 62-km Baltoro Glacier flows past their bases — one of the few places on Earth where four eight-thousanders are visible simultaneously from one viewpoint (Concordia).

question: The Pamir Mountains of Tajikistan are often called 'the Roof of the World'. The range is a knot where the Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, and Tian Shan mountain ranges all converge. What city near the southern edge of the Pamirs is the capital of Tajikistan?
context: The Pamir Highway (M41) — the second-highest international road on Earth — runs north-south through the range, climbing to 4,655 metres at the Ak-Baital Pass. The Pamir Knot is geologically the most extreme uplift on Earth outside the main Himalayan crest.

question: Stretching about 2,500 km across Central Asia, the 'Celestial Mountains' separate the basins of Central Asia from the steppes of Kazakhstan and the Tarim Basin of China. Khan Tengri (7,010 m, the world's northernmost 7,000-er) is its iconic pyramid peak. What four countries does the range run through?
context: 'Tian Shan' is Chinese for 'celestial mountain'; the Russian name is similar. Kyrgyzstan is dominated by the Tian Shan — much of the country lies above 2,500 metres. Issyk-Kul, the world's second-largest mountain lake, sits in the eastern Tian Shan.

question: Down western North America runs a long ridge of mountains called the Rocky Mountains, which marks the continent's hydrological divide. Streams east of this divide flow toward the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico; streams west of it flow toward the Pacific. What is this divide called?
answer: The Continental Divide of the Americas
choices: The Continental Divide of the Americas
The Great Divide of the Americas
context: The Continental Divide actually runs the length of both Americas; in the Rocky Mountains it tracks the highest crests. At Triple Divide Peak in Glacier National Park, water from three sides of one mountain flows to three different oceans (Pacific, Gulf, Hudson Bay).

question: The Appalachian Mountains in eastern North America were once a massive range — taller than the modern Himalayas — formed about 480 million years ago. They have eroded for hundreds of millions of years to their present modest height. They are sometimes the oldest mountain range in North America. What range across the Atlantic was once part of the same mountain belt?
context: Pangaea reconstructions show the Appalachian and Caledonian ranges as continuous; Pangaea's breakup tore them apart. The Atlas Mountains may also have been continuous with the Appalachians via the African plate, though that connection is less direct.

question: Stretching about 2,500 km across northwest Africa, this range separates the Mediterranean coast and Sahara Desert. Its highest peak, Toubkal in Morocco, rises 4,167 metres — high enough to hold snow most of the year despite the African latitude. The Berber name for these mountains involves a Greek myth. What is the link?
answer: Greek myth: the Titan Atlas held up the sky here
choices: Greek myth: the Titan Atlas held up the sky here
Greek myth: Hercules killed the Nemean lion here
Greek myth: Perseus turned Atlas to stone here
Greek myth: Prometheus was chained here
context: Both Greek versions are sometimes told: the Titan Atlas held up the heavens, or Perseus showed him the Gorgon's head and turned him to stone (becoming the mountains). The Atlas range provides the orographic lift that creates Morocco's relatively wet northwest — without it, the Sahara would extend to the Mediterranean.

question: In South Africa and Lesotho rises a steep basalt escarpment about 1,000 km long, with peaks over 3,400 metres and waterfalls in the wet season. The Zulu name means 'barrier of upward-pointing spears'. What is the modern English name?
context: The Drakensberg sandstone caves hold the largest concentration of San (Bushman) rock paintings in the world — over 35,000 individual images in about 600 sites, painted from perhaps 8,000 years ago into the 19th century. UNESCO World Heritage 2000.

question: The Southern Alps run 500 km down New Zealand's South Island. On the wet western flank, glaciers descend to within 250 metres of the sea — among the lowest temperate latitudes that any glacier reaches. The most famous fjord on the western coast was carved by these glaciers. What is it called?
context: Mitre Peak rises 1,692 metres straight from Milford Sound's water — one of the highest cliff-to-fjord drops anywhere. Westland gets over 6,000 mm of rain a year; this is what feeds the Franz Josef and Fox glaciers down to 250 m elevation. The Tasman Sea cooled by the West Coast Current contributes.

question: The largest hot desert on Earth covers about 9 million square kilometres of North Africa. Cave paintings and dry riverbeds show that 6,000 years ago this region was savanna with lakes, hippos, and human pastoralists. The same change — wet to dry — happens cyclically on roughly which time scale?
choices: About every 1 million years (long-term climate cycle)
Never — the Sahara has always been dry
context: Earth's axial precession (the wobble of the spin axis) shifts which hemisphere gets the strongest summer sun, in turn shifting the rains. In about 13,000 years, the Sahara may again be savanna. The 'African Humid Period' (15,000-5,000 years ago) was the last green phase.

question: In southeastern Morocco, the Sahara forms a region of golden sand dunes up to 150 metres tall. The dunes are alive — they migrate slowly with the wind. Camel caravans take tourists through them. What is this dune field called?
context: An 'erg' is an Arabic word for a sand-sea — a continuous mass of sand dunes. Most of the Sahara is actually rocky 'hamada' or gravel plain ('reg'); only about 20% is sand erg. Erg Chebbi is photogenic precisely because it is unusually concentrated and tall.

question: In central Asia stretches a cold desert of about 1.3 million square kilometres across northern China and southern Mongolia. Winters drop to -40°C; summers reach +40°C. The native two-humped, woolly camel (about 1,000 left in the wild) is endemic. What is it called?
context: All domestic two-humped camels are Bactrian; the wild Bactrian is a separate species (Camelus ferus) only recently recognised, living in a protected reserve in the Gobi. The Gobi is the largest desert in Asia and the fifth-largest in the world.

question: In western China's Tarim Basin lies one of the largest sand deserts in the world — its name is variously translated 'place of no return' or 'desert of death'. The Silk Road split into northern and southern routes to skirt it; almost no travellers crossed straight through. What is the desert called?
context: The Taklamakan has produced some of the world's best-preserved mummies — the Tarim mummies, some 4,000 years old, with intact red and blond hair and woolen tartans (looking Caucasian, raising questions about ancient migration). The Taklamakan crossings remain rare today; the Silk Road oasis cities still ring its edges.

question: In the southern Arabian Peninsula lies the largest continuous sand desert in the world — about 650,000 sq km of dunes, with no permanent rivers, lakes, or settlements. Wilfred Thesiger crossed it twice in 1946-1948 by camel. What is it called?
context: The Rub' al Khali sits inside Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman, and Yemen. Dunes here reach 250 metres. Underneath lies one of the world's largest oil reserves — Saudi Aramco's Shaybah, Empty Quarter field. The 1971 Apollo lunar landing site selection committee studied the Empty Quarter as a Moon-like training ground.

question: Stretching across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa, this red-sand 'thirstland' is technically a semi-desert — it gets 5-25 cm of rain a year, enough for grass and acacia trees in places. The indigenous San (Bushmen) have lived here as hunter-gatherers for tens of thousands of years. What is the desert called?
context: Okavango Delta, in northern Botswana, is a vast inland wetland where the Okavango River disappears into the Kalahari sands. The San speak languages with click consonants — among the oldest language families on Earth. The 1980 film 'The Gods Must Be Crazy' was filmed in the Kalahari.

question: Along the Atlantic coast of Namibia stretches a desert that may be the oldest on Earth — arid for at least 55 million years. Massive dunes (some 380 metres tall) reach right down to the ocean; cold ocean currents prevent rain from forming. What current is responsible?
context: The Benguela Current upwells cold water along Namibia's coast, cooling the air and preventing the rising-air rainfall typical of warm coasts. Fog from the cold ocean meets warm desert air daily; species like the Welwitschia plant and the fog-basking beetle drink the fog water.

question: The northern Namibian coast, where the Namib Desert meets the cold Benguela Current, is one of the world's most dangerous shorelines for ships. Hundreds of wrecks rust in the surf; the only land animals that can survive the area are desert-adapted elephants and lions. What is this coast called?
context: Fog combined with offshore shoals and powerful surf has wrecked ships from Portuguese vessels in the 1500s to fishing boats today. Whale bones once mantled the beach, giving the coast its English name; the Khoisan name was 'The Land God Made in Anger'.

question: On the Pacific coast of Chile and Peru sits the driest non-polar desert on Earth — some weather stations have never recorded a measurable rainfall in over 50 years of records. The desert is so arid that NASA uses it to test Mars rovers. What rain shadow effect plus what current cause the dryness?
answer: Andes rain shadow plus Humboldt cold current
choices: Andes rain shadow plus Humboldt cold current
Atlas rain shadow plus Canary cold current
Sierra Madre rain shadow plus California current
Drakensberg rain shadow plus Benguela current
context: The Andes block moisture from the Atlantic; the Humboldt Current cools coastal air so it cannot rise to make rain. Some places — Calama, Arica — average under 1 mm of rain per year. The Atacama also has the world's clearest skies; the ALMA observatory operates there.

question: At 5,000 metres in the Chilean Atacama Desert sits one of the most advanced ground-based astronomical facilities on Earth — 66 radio dish antennas (12 metres each) on a moveable platform, observing at millimetre wavelengths to peer through dust clouds and detect distant galaxies and forming stars. What is it called?
context: ALMA went into full operation in 2013. The dry, high site is crucial: water vapour in air absorbs millimetre-wavelength light, so the higher and drier, the better. The instruments are too sensitive to be operated by humans nearby — staff control them from a base camp 30 km lower.

question: South of latitude 38, the Andes' rain shadow makes eastern Argentina a vast cold desert — strong winds, sparse vegetation, sheep ranches and oil derricks. The region runs to Tierra del Fuego. What is this Argentine region called?
context: The name 'Patagonia' was bestowed by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520 — supposedly from a giant-like figure called Patagon in a Spanish novel he had read. The native Tehuelche were tall by Spanish standards, hence the comparison. Patagonia includes both the Argentine east and a thin strip of Chile.

question: In the southwestern United States lies the smallest North American desert (about 124,000 sq km). Its signature plant is a spiky tree-yucca that Mormon settlers thought resembled the prophet Joshua raising his arms to the sky. What is this desert called?
context: Joshua trees only grow in the Mojave and its borders. The desert sits between the Sierra Nevada and Colorado Plateau; Death Valley is its most extreme corner. Las Vegas is the largest city in the Mojave; the Mojave Air & Space Port is where SpaceShipOne was built.

question: Spanning parts of Arizona, California, and northwestern Mexico, this desert has the highest plant and animal diversity of any North American desert — including a unique columnar cactus (Carnegiea gigantea) that grows up to 12 metres and lives 150-200 years. What is the cactus called?
context: Saguaros do not grow their first 'arms' until about age 75. They produce night-blooming white flowers (Arizona's state flower) pollinated by lesser long-nosed bats. The species is protected — destroying or moving one in Arizona is a felony.

question: Most of the interior of Australia is dry, hot, and sparsely populated — a region that English-speaking Australians call by an evocative two-word name. The legendary 'red centre' lies at the heart of it. What is this region called?
context: Coober Pedy, in the South Australian Outback, is the world's largest opal-mining town — most residents live in 'dugout' houses excavated underground to escape the heat. Most of the Outback receives less than 250 mm of rain per year; some places only briefly turn green after rare floods.

question: In southeastern Iran, this desert holds the record for the highest ground-surface temperature ever measured by satellite — 80.8°C (177°F), set in 2018. Inland from the dunes are vast Yardang plateaus carved by wind erosion. What is the desert called?
context: Air temperature there is more moderate (still very high). The Lut's salt-flats reach over 70°C surface temperature several months a year. The Kaluts — vast wind-carved ridges in the desert — are some of Earth's most striking aeolian landscapes.

question: Antarctica is technically a desert — it receives less than 200 mm of precipitation per year (mostly as snow that accumulates rather than melting). It is the largest desert on Earth — about 14 million square kilometres. What is the average annual precipitation at the South Pole itself?
context: The South Pole gets perhaps 50-80 mm of snow per year, which compacts to under 10 mm water equivalent. The continent's coastal margins get more snow. The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert; the Antarctic Dry Valleys (no ice cover) are arguably the driest place on Earth — no rain in millions of years in some spots.

question: Antarctica is roughly the size of the United States and Mexico combined. Its ice sheet — some 4.5 km thick at its thickest — holds about what percentage of all freshwater on Earth?
context: If all the ice melted, sea level would rise by about 58 metres globally. Antarctica's ice has been there for at least 30 million years. The continent is covered by ice 98%; only mountain peaks and the Antarctic Peninsula coast are ice-free.

question: Within Antarctica sits the largest ice-free region of the continent — three valleys near McMurdo Sound where strong katabatic winds prevent snow from settling. NASA tests Mars probes here. Some of the rocks in the Dry Valleys may not have been beneath ice or snow for millions of years. What are they called?
context: The valleys hold permanently frozen lakes whose surface ice never thaws but whose deep water is liquid (and saline) below. Algal mats grow under the ice in some lakes — alien-life analogues for Mars or Europa research.

question: Beneath about 4 km of ice in eastern Antarctica sits a freshwater lake roughly the size of Lake Ontario, sealed off from the surface for perhaps 15-25 million years. Russian drilling in 2012 reached its surface. What is this lake called?
context: Vostok is one of about 400 subglacial Antarctic lakes. Penetrating Vostok without contaminating it has been controversial — Russian drillers used kerosene-Freon antifreeze that critics worried might pollute the pristine water. Microorganisms in retrieved water are debated.

question: The smallest and shallowest of the world's five oceans is also the only one that ships cannot easily cross — surface ice has historically prevented routine navigation. Recent ice retreat has made some routes seasonally open. What is this ocean called?
context: The Arctic Ocean covers about 14 million sq km — about half the next-smallest, the Southern. Its summer minimum sea-ice extent has declined by about 13% per decade since 1979. The Northwest Passage and Northern Sea Route are now seasonally navigable.

question: Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent, the North Pole sits on drifting sea ice on the surface of an ocean. Beneath the pole the seabed is about how deep?
context: The seabed at the North Pole is part of the Lomonosov Ridge or its surroundings, dropping into the Eurasian Basin. Russia, Canada, Norway, Denmark (Greenland) all claim portions of the Arctic seabed; UN Convention on the Law of the Sea adjudicates.

question: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent, and over 80% of its surface is covered by an ice sheet up to how thick at its centre?
context: The Greenland ice sheet has been there for at least 1 million years. Recent melting has accelerated — the sheet is losing about 280 billion tons of ice per year on average. If completely melted, global sea level would rise about 7 metres.

question: On 14 April 1912 at 11:40 PM ship time, the RMS Titanic struck an iceberg about 400 km southeast of Newfoundland. The iceberg had drifted south from a Greenland glacier on which famous current?
context: The Labrador Current is cold and southwest-flowing along the Canadian coast; it carries thousands of icebergs each spring from Baffin Bay south into the North Atlantic shipping lanes. The 1912 disaster led to the International Ice Patrol, which monitors and warns ships to this day.

question: Above the Earth's polar regions, charged particles from the Sun stream along the magnetic-field lines into the upper atmosphere, where they collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms and excite them to glow in greens, pinks, reds, and violets. What is the northern version of this phenomenon called?
context: Green is the most common colour: oxygen at about 100 km altitude. Red comes from oxygen at very high altitude (200-300 km). Purple/pink comes from nitrogen. Aurora is most visible between geomagnetic latitudes 60-75. The solar maximum (every 11 years) increases aurora frequency.

question: Across the high Arctic — Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada — soil that has remained frozen for at least two years (often for thousands) is called permafrost. As it thaws, it releases what greenhouse gas trapped in ancient organic matter?
context: Permafrost holds an estimated 1,500 gigatons of carbon — roughly twice what is in the atmosphere currently. As it thaws, microbial decomposition releases CO2 in oxygen-rich conditions and methane in waterlogged conditions. Both are major climate-feedback concerns.

question: On the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard sits a deep-frozen vault built into a sandstone mountain — opened in 2008 to hold backup copies of crop seeds from genebanks around the world, as insurance against catastrophic loss. The vault now holds about 1.2 million seed varieties. About how cold is it kept?
context: Even if all the freezers fail, the surrounding permafrost stays well below freezing year-round. The vault has already had one withdrawal — Syria's genebank duplicates were retrieved in 2015 after the original was damaged in the civil war.

question: In southern Argentine Patagonia, a 5-km-wide tongue of ice descends from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field to Lake Argentino, periodically blocking the lake. Pressure builds; eventually a spectacular dam break occurs as ice collapses into the lake — a tourist event that draws huge crowds. What is this glacier called?
context: Perito Moreno is one of the few major glaciers in the world not retreating significantly — its terminus is roughly stable. The dam-rupture event has happened 23 times since 1947, sometimes more than a decade apart. Most other Patagonian ice-field glaciers are retreating rapidly.

question: The Amazon Rainforest covers about 5.5 million sq km — 60% in Brazil, the rest spread across Peru, Colombia, and six other countries. Often called 'the lungs of the planet', it actually produces and consumes about the same amount of oxygen. What is the more accurate function it plays in the carbon cycle?
answer: A vast carbon sink — net absorber of CO2 (until recently)
choices: A vast carbon sink — net absorber of CO2 (until recently)
A net carbon source — always releasing more CO2 than absorbing
Climate-neutral — neither source nor sink of CO2
An oxygen-only producer with no role in CO2
context: Recent studies show parts of the Amazon, especially the southeast, have become net carbon sources because of deforestation and fires. The Amazon still functions as a carbon sink in much of its western and northern range. About 17% has been deforested since 1970; tipping-point estimates start at 20-25%.

question: Africa's largest contiguous rainforest covers about 200 million hectares across six countries — Cameroon, Central African Republic, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, and Gabon. What is its informal name?
context: The Congo Basin's forests are second only to the Amazon in area and biodiversity. The basin holds about 30 million people. Forest elephants (a smaller distinct species from savanna elephants), forest buffalo, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos, and okapi all live here.

question: Around the Arctic Circle, a belt of dense conifer forest covers about 17% of Earth's land surface — making it the largest terrestrial biome. The Russian name for the forest is widely used. What is it?
context: Taiga (Russian for 'forest') circles the northern hemisphere across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, and Russia. Spruce, fir, pine, and larch dominate; the soils are acidic and shallow. The taiga absorbs and stores enormous amounts of carbon — about 14% of the world's terrestrial carbon.

question: Along the foggy northern California coast grow the tallest trees on Earth — coastal redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) up to 115 metres tall. Their height limit is set largely by the difficulty of pulling water that far up against gravity. The tallest known living individual is called what?
context: Hyperion's exact location is kept secret to protect it from tourists. The redwoods have only one close relative, the dawn redwood (Metasequoia, native to a small area of China). Coastal redwoods need the marine fog that drips onto their canopies for hydration.

question: In California's Sierra Nevada, an inland cousin of the coastal redwood grows shorter but enormously thicker. The largest tree on Earth by trunk volume — 1,486 cubic metres, weighing about 1,200 tons — has a name. What is it?
context: General Sherman is about 2,200-2,700 years old. Giant sequoias only grow in about 70 isolated groves on the western Sierra Nevada slopes, mostly in Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks. The biggest trees can sprout from a seed lighter than a grain of rice.

question: In the dry White Mountains and Inyo National Forest of California grow the oldest non-clonal organisms on Earth — twisted, half-dead-looking pines whose oldest living individual is over 4,800 years old. What species is this?
context: The oldest documented bristlecone — Methuselah — germinated about 2832 BC. Its exact location is kept secret. The trees grow only millimetres a year, in very dense, resinous wood that resists decay. A still-older tree (5,062 years in 2017) was found nearby but its location and identifier have not been disclosed.

question: In Utah's Fishlake National Forest, a clonal stand of quaking aspen — all genetically identical, all interconnected by a single root system — covers 43 hectares with about 47,000 stems. By total mass, this single organism may be the largest on Earth. What is it called?
context: Pando is estimated at 14,000 to 80,000 years old depending on method. Stems above ground rarely live more than 150 years; the root system is what carries the genetic identity. Recent studies show Pando is in decline — overgrazing by deer that no longer fear extinct wolves keeps new shoots from surviving.

question: Off the southeast coast of Africa, the world's fourth-largest island has unique vegetation — about 85% of its plant species are found nowhere else. The most famous is a thick-trunked tree of which six of the eight species in the world grow only here. What tree is this?
context: Madagascar separated from mainland Africa about 165 million years ago, then from India about 88 million years ago. The 'Avenue of the Baobabs' near Morondava — a road lined with 800-year-old Adansonia grandidieri trees — is one of the most-photographed sites on the island.

question: On a remote Yemeni island in the Arabian Sea grows a bizarre umbrella-shaped tree whose red sap was used in medieval medicine and dye-making. About one-third of all plant species on the island grow nowhere else; the island has been isolated for millions of years. What is this tree called?
context: Socotra also holds the cucumber tree, the desert rose with bulbous trunk, and bizarre frankincense species. The island is sometimes called 'the Galapagos of the Indian Ocean' for its level of endemism. Recent civil war and Saudi-led conflict have made Socotra hard to visit.

question: In the western Pacific east of the Mariana Islands runs the deepest known place in the ocean. The bottom is about 10,935 metres below sea level — so deep that Everest, inverted, would still leave about 2 km of water above its peak. What is the deepest single point called?
context: Challenger Deep is named after the HMS Challenger expedition that found it in 1875. The first crewed descent (1960) was by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe Trieste; Cameron and Bezos have also descended since. Pressure at the bottom is over 1,000 atmospheres.

question: The Pacific Ocean covers about 165 million sq km — more than all the land area of Earth combined. It is also the deepest ocean and holds about how much of all the water on Earth?
context: The Pacific's name comes from Magellan, who reached it after Atlantic storms and the Strait of Magellan and found calm seas — pacifico in Spanish. It is also slowly shrinking as Atlantic spreads and Pacific subducts under the Americas and Asia.

question: A warm-water current carries heat from the Gulf of Mexico across the North Atlantic, helping keep northwestern Europe far warmer than its latitude alone would suggest — London at 51° N is much milder than Calgary at 51° N. What is this current called?
context: The Gulf Stream is about 100 km wide and transports more water than all the rivers on Earth combined. Climate change projections include possible weakening of the AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) that drives it; a major shutdown would be disastrous for European climate.

question: Off Japan's east coast flows a warm western-boundary current — the Pacific equivalent of the Gulf Stream. Its Japanese name means 'black current' (for the dark, clear, nutrient-poor tropical water). What is it called?
context: Kuroshio brings warm water and species north along Japan. It meets the cold Oyashio (Arctic-origin) current off northeast Japan, creating one of the most biologically productive zones on Earth — the Sanriku-Oki fishing ground.

question: Along the western coast of South America (mostly Peru and Chile) flows a cold north-flowing current that brings cold deep water to the surface (upwelling). The Humboldt feeds one of the world's most productive fisheries — accounting for nearly a fifth of all fish caught globally. What is the dominant fished species?
context: Anchoveta catch peaks at 8-10 million tons per year — among the largest single-species fisheries on Earth. Almost all becomes fishmeal for aquaculture and livestock feed. El Nino years collapse the upwelling and the anchoveta with it; the 1972 collapse triggered a global protein crisis.

question: Off the northeast coast of Australia stretches the largest living structure on Earth — a 2,300-km-long, 344,000-sq-km mosaic of about 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, visible from space. What is it called?
context: The Great Barrier Reef hosts about 9,000 species. Coral bleaching — caused by warmer water expelling symbiotic algae — has hit it severely in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022. Roughly half of the reef's shallow-water coral cover has been lost since the mid-1990s; recovery happens between events but capacity is shrinking.

question: The largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere runs about 290 km off the coast of Belize. UNESCO World Heritage. Inside the reef sits a near-perfect circular sinkhole over 300 metres across — a former cave system that collapsed when sea level rose at the end of the last ice age. What is the sinkhole called?
context: The Blue Hole is 124 metres deep. Stalactites that hang from its underwater overhangs prove it was a dry cave at one point — about 14,000-153,000 years ago. Jacques Cousteau named it one of the 'top five scuba diving sites in the world' after exploring it in 1971.

question: Between Africa and Arabia stretches a narrow body of water that is widening by about 1-2 cm per year as the Arabian Plate splits from Africa. Geologists project that in some tens of millions of years it will be a full ocean. What is this body of water called?
context: The Red Sea is on a divergent boundary — same kind of boundary as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, but earlier in the process. The eponymous 'red' may come from seasonal cyanobacterial blooms or from a translation of the Greek 'Eritrean' (probably 'south', not 'red').

question: The Black Sea is unusual among Earth's seas: below about 200 metres depth, its water is essentially devoid of oxygen — anoxic, due to limited circulation with the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus and high freshwater inflow. What practical effect does this have on shipwrecks below 200 metres?
answer: Wooden hulls and organic materials are exceptionally well preserved
choices: Wooden hulls and organic materials are exceptionally well preserved
Wooden hulls dissolve much faster than in oxygenated water
Metals corrode much faster due to sulfide chemistry
Anoxic water is biologically active and consumes wood
context: The Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project has discovered Byzantine, Roman, Greek, and Ottoman ships at depths down to 2 km, with intact wood, rigging, and even fragments of cargo. The anoxic Black Sea is one of the world's most important time capsules for ancient maritime history.

question: Between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in Canada lies a long narrow bay where the average tidal range is the largest on Earth — about 12 metres, with spring tides exceeding 16 metres in places. The bay's resonant frequency happens to match the tidal cycle. What is this bay called?
context: About 100 billion tons of water enter and leave the Bay of Fundy on each tide — more than all the rivers in the world combined. Reversing rapids and tidal bores happen at the heads of the bay's branches. Fundy is named for 'fondo' (Portuguese for 'deep' or 'bottom').

question: In the central North Atlantic floats the only sea on Earth with no land boundaries — instead, four ocean currents (the North Atlantic Gyre) circle around its still water. The sea is filled with floating yellow-brown algae for which it is named. What algae?
context: European and American eels both spawn somewhere in the Sargasso. The sea hosts a unique ecosystem of fish and invertebrates adapted to the floating sargassum. Recent years have seen blooms of sargassum so large they wash ashore in the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico in mats kilometres long.

question: In northern Arizona, the Colorado River has cut through 2 billion years of geological history into the Colorado Plateau, exposing rock layers from the Vishnu Schist (1.8 billion years old) at the bottom to the Kaibab Limestone at the top. About how many million years has this carving taken?
context: The canyon is about 446 km long, up to 29 km wide, and 1.8 km deep at its deepest. The relatively rapid carving — geologically speaking — was made possible by the plateau being uplifted while the river course was already in place, forcing the river to cut down as the land rose.

question: In southwestern Utah, an amphitheatre of pink-orange rock holds the densest concentration of tall thin spires anywhere on Earth — thousands of them, formed by frost wedging and water erosion. What are these spires called?
context: Bryce Canyon's hoodoos form in the Claron Formation — soft limestone capped by harder rock that resists weathering. The cap-rock protects a narrow tower beneath until eventually weathering tips it. Paiute legend says the hoodoos are people turned to stone by a trickster god.

question: In southeastern Utah and northeastern Arizona, on Navajo Nation land, isolated sandstone monoliths rise as much as 300 metres straight up from a flat desert floor. The site became one of the world's most photographed landscapes after John Ford filmed John Wayne westerns here. What are the monoliths called?
context: The visible monoliths are remnants of a once-continuous Permian sandstone plateau that has eroded around them. The Navajo (Dine) name is Tse'Bii'Ndzisgaii. Visitors enter via the Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park; the iconic 'Mittens' and Merrick Butte appear in countless westerns.

question: In southeastern Utah's Arches National Park stands a 16-metre freestanding sandstone arch — appearing on the Utah license plate. It looks impossibly thin and is the symbol of Utah's red rock country. What is it called?
context: The arch has stood for at least 80,000 years. Park rangers were photographed measuring it; concerns about thinning sections caused the closure of the area beneath. Landscape Arch (88 m span) is technically the longest arch in the park; a 22-metre section of it fell off in 1991.

question: On Navajo Nation land in northeastern Arizona, a narrow sandstone canyon carved by flash floods rises 20 metres tall with walls only metres wide. Sunlight at noon falls through narrow openings as 'sunbeams' onto the canyon floor, lighting up the swirled red walls. What is this canyon called?
context: Antelope Canyon's name comes from herds of pronghorn antelope that once grazed nearby. Flash floods can be deadly even in clear weather; eleven tourists died in a 1997 flash flood here. The canyon is only accessible with Navajo tour guides.

question: About 50,000 years ago, a 50-metre-wide iron-nickel meteorite struck a flat plateau in what is now northern Arizona, creating a 1.2-km-wide, 170-metre-deep bowl. The crater is one of the best-preserved on Earth — the dry climate has barely weathered it. About how big was the impactor?
context: The impact released energy equivalent to about 10 megatons of TNT. The Apollo astronauts trained at Meteor Crater for lunar geology. Daniel Barringer bought it in 1902 expecting to mine a buried iron meteorite worth millions; he died bankrupt — the meteor had vaporised on impact.

question: In central Anatolia, Turkey, volcanic ash from ancient eruptions of Mount Erciyes hardened into soft tuff that erosion has carved into spires sometimes capped by harder volcanic rock — creating thousands of tall, hat-topped pillars. Early Christians dug churches and even whole underground cities into the soft rock. What is the region called?
context: Beneath Cappadocia lies the Derinkuyu underground city — at least 11 levels deep, capacity for 20,000 people, with stables, churches, kitchens, and ventilation shafts. It was used by Christians fleeing Roman and later Muslim persecution. The fairy chimneys' caps are basalt; the pillars are tuff.

question: In western Turkey, hot mineral springs flowing down a hillside have deposited terraces of brilliant white travertine over millennia, creating a 'cotton castle' visible from kilometres away. The ancient Roman city of Hierapolis was built on top. What is the natural site called?
context: The terraced pools cascade for 2.7 km. The waters are about 35-100°C at the springs. UNESCO listed Pamukkale-Hierapolis as a Mixed Site in 1988. Tourist damage in the 1990s led to flow restrictions; some terraces were partly drying up.

question: On the Bolivian altiplano at 3,656 metres lies the largest salt flat on Earth — 10,582 sq km of nearly perfectly flat white salt crust over a brine pool. In the rainy season a thin layer of water turns the entire surface into a mirror reflecting the sky. What is the salt flat called?
context: The salt is about 10 metres thick on average and overlies about 11 lakes of brine. Beneath the brine lies an estimated 70% of the world's lithium reserves. The salt was deposited by the drying of prehistoric Lake Minchin, about 40,000 years ago.

question: On the northern coast of Northern Ireland, about 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns step out into the sea — the cooled and fractured top of a Paleogene lava flow about 60 million years ago. Local legend says the giant Finn MacCool built it to fight a Scottish giant. What is the formation called?
context: The columns formed as the lava cooled and contracted, naturally fracturing in a hexagonal pattern (closest to a honeycomb of equal-sized cells). A similar feature, Fingal's Cave on the Scottish island of Staffa, was once connected to the same lava flow before the Atlantic opened up.

question: In northeastern Wyoming rises a 265-metre-tall flat-topped igneous monolith that geologists believe is the eroded core of an ancient volcanic intrusion. Lakota and Cheyenne peoples consider it sacred. It featured prominently in the 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind. What is its name in English?
context: The Lakota name Mato Tipila ('Bear Lodge') reflects the legend that the tower's vertical scoring marks where a giant bear clawed it. President Theodore Roosevelt declared it the first U.S. National Monument in 1906. Climbers ascend its rock columns; a voluntary climbing ban honours indigenous spiritual practice in June.

question: In central Australia, a 348-metre-tall sandstone monolith rises sharply from the flat desert. It is the eroded tip of a much larger underground rock formation — most of the rock lies hidden below the surface. What kind of formation is it?
context: Uluru's iron content reddens at sunrise and sunset. Estimates of how much of the rock is below the surface vary — some say only about 10% is visible. Uluru and the nearby Kata Tjuta (the Olgas) are part of the same basement rock unit.

question: On the Filipino island of Bohol stand about 1,500 nearly identical conical limestone hills, about 30-50 metres tall. Their grass turns brown each dry season, giving the impression of a chocolate landscape. What kind of geological feature are they?
context: Tropical karst forms in humid climates where chemical weathering dissolves limestone faster than mechanical erosion. The Chocolate Hills are an unusual case where the hills are remarkably uniform; theories include uplifted ancient coral reefs eroded uniformly by groundwater.

question: In Western Australia, a 14-metre-tall, 100-metre-long granite outcrop forms a perfect curl like an enormous surf wave about to break. The 'wave' face has been carved over 2.7 billion years by chemical weathering followed by erosion. What is this rock called?
context: Wave Rock is part of the granite outcrop called Hyden Rock. Chemical weathering at the base of the rock, where groundwater pools, slowly hollowed out the curl shape; later erosion has revealed it as the rock emerged from soil. The streaks on the wall are mineral run-off from the weathering.

question: On the borders of Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana rises a 2,810-metre table mountain — a tepui, the world's oldest mountain plateau, separated from surrounding lowlands by cliffs 400-1,000 metres tall. The isolated summit hosts species found nowhere else on Earth. Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel borrowed its mystery for his book title. What was the book?
context: Roraima's flat summit is about 30 sq km. The tepui plateau hosts carnivorous plants and unique endemic species (a small frog, a cricket, a specialised bird). Climbers reach the summit via a 'natural staircase' on the Venezuelan side. The vegetation on top — adapted to extreme leaching of nutrients — is bizarre.

question: In Yellowstone National Park, the largest hot spring in the United States — 110 metres across, deeper than a six-storey building — circles concentric rings of brilliant blue, green, yellow, orange, and red. The colours come from heat-loving microorganisms forming different bands at different water temperatures. What is the spring called?
context: The blue centre is sterile (too hot for microbes, about 87°C). Cyanobacteria and other thermophiles thrive at progressively cooler temperatures, each species producing different carotenoid pigments. The orange ring is dominated by Synechococcus elongatus; the green by chlorophyll-producing thermophiles.

question: Yellowstone's most famous geyser erupts every 60-110 minutes (interval varying after the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake), shooting boiling water 30-55 metres into the air for about 3 minutes. What is the geyser called?
context: Old Faithful is not the largest or the most regular geyser, but it is the most predictably regular major geyser. Steamboat (also in Yellowstone) is the tallest geyser on Earth when it does erupt — up to 110 metres — but it can go years between eruptions. About 300 of the 500 active geysers on Earth are in Yellowstone.

question: In southwest Iceland, a hot spring that erupts gives the entire phenomenon its name in English. Records of its eruptions go back to 1294. Its current eruptions are sporadic; nearby Strokkur is more reliable, erupting every 5-10 minutes. What is the original spring called?
context: The English word 'geyser' derives from this Icelandic spring — from Old Norse 'geysa', to gush. Geysir's eruptions stopped largely after silica was added to its plumbing in the 20th century, in unsuccessful attempts to revive eruptions. Earthquakes occasionally restart it briefly.

question: In Ethiopia's Danakil Depression — one of the lowest points on land at 125 metres below sea level — hot acidic mineral pools cluster on a sulfur-coated salt plain. Iron, salt, sulfur, and bacteria turn the pools brilliant yellow, green, orange, and white. The air temperature averages 35°C year-round, among the hottest inhabited places. What is this site called?
context: Dallol sits over a still-active volcanic complex. The Afar people mine salt here in traditional camel-caravan operations. Visitors come on guided trips with armed escort — the Eritrean border is contested and bandit attacks happen. Dallol is among the most extreme environments on Earth's surface.

question: Occasionally at sunset over the ocean, the last sliver of the setting sun appears for a fraction of a second as brilliant green before disappearing. The effect is caused by Earth's atmosphere acting as a prism, refracting the shorter wavelengths more. What is this phenomenon called?
context: The green flash requires a clear horizon and very stable atmospheric conditions. Sailors and pilots have reported it for centuries; Jules Verne wrote a romantic novel about it in 1882. Captured on video most reliably at high mountain summits looking down on a flat horizon.

question: On hot tarmac on a desert road, a shimmering 'puddle' that disappears as you approach is actually an image of the sky bent into your eyes by a layer of very hot air just above the road. What is this kind of mirage called?
context: Inferior mirages put the false image below the real object (the sky is below your eye-line in the puddle effect). Superior mirages put the image above the real object — and can produce phantom ships, distant cliffs, and the famous Fata Morgana of the Strait of Messina.

question: Sometimes after a rain shower you can see two concentric rainbows — a brighter inner one with red on top, and a fainter outer one with red on the bottom (colours reversed). Between them lies a darker band where no rainbow forms. What is the darker band called?
context: Alexander of Aphrodisias described it around 200 AD. The primary rainbow comes from one internal reflection inside each raindrop; the secondary from two reflections. The dark band is the angular gap where neither one nor two reflections puts light into your eye.

question: On full-moon nights at Victoria Falls in Africa, when mist from the falls fills the air, a rainbow forms in the moonlight — a pale arc against the dark sky. What is this phenomenon called?
context: Moonbows are physically identical to ordinary rainbows but appear much fainter because moonlight is about 400,000 times dimmer than sunlight. They appear nearly white to the naked eye; long-exposure photography reveals colour. Victoria Falls and a few other waterfall locations are reliable moonbow spots.

question: On cold winter days, two bright spots of light may appear flanking the sun at the same elevation, about 22° away on each side. Hexagonal ice crystals in high cirrus clouds act as tiny prisms refracting the light. What are these spots called?
context: Sun dogs form a triple image of the sun. The Latin name parhelion means 'beside the sun'. The same crystals can also produce a 22° halo around the sun — a faint ring at the same radius.

question: Each year in early June, a massive seasonal wind shift brings the rains that water about a fifth of the world's people in South Asia. The summer monsoon arrives first on the southwest tip of India, in the state of Kerala. What is the rough date of arrival?
context: Indian agriculture and economic life still rotates around the monsoon's onset. Failure or weakness causes drought and famine; excess causes flooding. The mechanism — solar heating of the Tibetan plateau drawing in moist air from the Indian Ocean — is a major topic in modern climate science.

question: Every 2-7 years, a band of warm Pacific water spreads eastward toward South America, suppressing the cold Humboldt upwelling and disrupting weather across the planet. The effect was first noticed by Peruvian fishermen who named it after the Christ child because it usually peaked around Christmas. What is it called?
context: El Nino changes rainfall around the Pacific Rim — drought in Australia and Indonesia, floods in Peru and Ecuador, a milder hurricane season in the Atlantic, more storms in the eastern Pacific. La Nina is the opposite phase — anomalously cold east Pacific.

question: Between the equator and about 30 degrees north and south, steady easterly winds blow from the higher pressure subtropical highs toward the equator. European sailing ships used them to cross the Atlantic toward the New World. What are these winds called?
context: Columbus rode the trades west. The name 'trade' comes from an obsolete English meaning of 'track' or 'path' — the winds blow along a regular path. The trade winds converge near the equator in the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where they spawn most of the world's tropical thunderstorms.

question: Between latitudes 40°S and 50°S in the Southern Hemisphere, westerly winds blow uninterrupted around the globe with no continents to slow them. Mariners on the clipper-ship route from Europe to Australia took advantage of these winds; they also drive the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. What are they called?
context: The names extend with latitude: the 50s are 'Furious', the 60s are 'Screaming'. The Southern Ocean has no land between South Africa, Australia, and South America at this latitude, so wind builds up with nothing to break it. Clippers loaded with wool ran 'east-about' around the globe.

question: Between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River in central North America, cold dry air from Canada repeatedly meets warm humid air from the Gulf of Mexico, producing the densest cluster of tornadoes on Earth. About how many tornadoes hit the United States in an average year?
context: Tornado Alley typically covers Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, and parts of South Dakota. The most destructive tornadoes (EF5) are concentrated here. The U.S. has more tornadoes than any other country in the world; Bangladesh and Argentina also have substantial activity.

question: On the eastern (lee) side of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta and Montana, a warm dry wind sometimes sweeps down from the mountains in winter, raising temperatures by 20-30°C in hours and melting snow. Native peoples called it 'snow-eater'. What is the meteorological name?
context: Chinook is descended cold air that has dropped its moisture on the windward side of the mountains and adiabatically warmed as it sank. Similar warm-dry foehn winds happen on the lee of many mountain ranges worldwide; the Chinook is North America's example.

question: Each winter from late November to mid-March, a dry, dust-laden wind blows from the Sahara southwest across West Africa, dropping humidity to single-digit percentages and dimming the sun. What is this wind called?
context: The Harmattan dust can reach as far as the Caribbean — actually fertilising the Amazon basin with mineral-rich Saharan dust that has crossed the Atlantic. The wind dries skin and lips painfully; the haze is sometimes thick enough to ground flights.

question: In the spring (typically April-June), a hot dry sand-laden wind from the Sahara sweeps over Egypt for about fifty days, lifting temperatures by 20°C, scouring crops, and reducing visibility. The wind is named for its duration. What is it called in Arabic?
context: The Khamsin can blow for several days in a row at gale strength. It is the same kind of wind as the Sirocco in Italy and the Sharav in Israel; the name is regional. Egyptian farmers historically considered the Khamsin a major threat to spring harvests.

question: Surrounding each pole in the stratosphere swirls a circumpolar low-pressure system of frigid air. When it weakens or splits, lobes of Arctic air can spill far south, causing record cold in regions like the central United States or Europe. What is this called?
context: The polar vortex weakens when stratospheric warming events happen — a wave of warming travels from the tropics. Famous polar vortex breakouts hit the U.S. in January 2014 and again in February 2021, freezing Texas. Climate change appears to be making such breakouts more common, paradoxically.

question: About 1,000 km off Ecuador's coast in the Pacific lie volcanic islands where Darwin spent five weeks in 1835 observing the unique wildlife — finches with diverse beak shapes, marine and land iguanas, giant tortoises, flightless cormorants. What is this archipelago called?
context: The islands sit on a hotspot like Hawaii — each volcanic island ages as the Nazca plate carries it eastward away from the source. Darwin's observations contributed to On the Origin of Species (1859); the finches' adaptive radiation has been further studied by Peter and Rosemary Grant since the 1970s.

question: On New Zealand's remote outer islands lives the world's largest and longest-lived parrot — a nocturnal, flightless, ground-dwelling species that smells strongly of honey and moss. It evolved in the absence of mammals; introduced rats and possums nearly drove it extinct. How many remain (as of 2024)?
context: The kakapo population has been growing slowly under intensive conservation management. Each bird has a name and is tracked individually. They live on predator-free offshore islands. The species breeds only when certain native trees mast — every 2-4 years.

question: On a handful of small Indonesian islands lives the largest lizard on Earth — about 3 metres long, 90 kg, with a venomous bite and a willingness to ambush water buffaloes, deer, and occasionally humans. About how many remain in the wild?
context: Komodo dragons live on Komodo, Rinca, Padar, Flores, and Gili Motang in the Lesser Sundas. They survived on these isolated islands; mainland Australian relatives went extinct in the Holocene. They are now the largest predators of Komodo National Park.

question: In northern Botswana, the Okavango River — which flows about 1,600 km from the Angolan highlands — never reaches the sea. Instead it spreads out over the Kalahari sands in a vast seasonal wetland of channels, papyrus swamps, and 'islands' (some are anthills). Elephants, lions, leopards, and hippos all live here. What kind of geographic feature is this?
context: The Okavango Delta is one of the few major endorheic deltas on Earth (water has no outlet to sea). The annual flood pulse drives ecological activity — wildlife congregates in dry season around the persistent channels. UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site since 2014.

question: Across the plains of Tanzania and Kenya, about 1.5 million wildebeest, 200,000 zebras, and 500,000 Thomson's gazelles move in an annual cycle following seasonal rains and grass. The herd crosses the Grumeti and Mara rivers — where huge Nile crocodiles wait. What is this cycle called?
context: The migration's exact timing varies — it tracks rainfall, not the calendar. About 250,000 wildebeest die each year during the cycle from drowning, predation, or exhaustion. The Serengeti National Park and Maasai Mara National Reserve combine to protect the entire migration route.

question: About 252 million years ago, the largest known volcanic eruption sequence in Earth's history covered some 7 million square kilometres of Siberia in basaltic lava over about 1-2 million years. The CO2 release drove climate change that caused the Permian-Triassic mass extinction — Earth's worst — killing about 96% of marine species. What is this lava province called?
context: 'Traps' is from the Swedish 'trappa' (stair) referring to the stepped landscape of the eroded basalt flows. The Siberian Traps eruption injected so much CO2 and sulfur into the atmosphere that ocean acidification, anoxia, and global warming all contributed to the extinction.

question: In certain bays in Puerto Rico, the Maldives, and Jamaica, swimmers stir the water at night and the wake glows brilliant blue-green. Microscopic single-celled algae produce light when disturbed — a defensive response thought to startle predators or attract bigger fish to eat them. What are these organisms?
context: Bahia Bioluminiscente in Vieques, Puerto Rico, holds the highest concentration ever measured — about 700,000 dinoflagellates per gallon. The reaction uses luciferin and luciferase, the same enzyme family that lights up fireflies. Light pollution reduces the visible effect; the brightest experiences are away from cities.

question: In Kentucky stretches the world's longest cave system — over 686 km of surveyed passages on multiple levels, with new sections still being discovered. The cave formed in limestone, partly capped by a layer of insoluble sandstone that protected the bedrock from collapse. What is this cave system called?
context: Mammoth Cave's history of human use goes back 4,000 years. Native Americans mined gypsum and crystals from it. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981. The cave is roughly twice as long as the second-longest known system (Sistema Sac Actun in Mexico, mostly underwater).

question: In the Western Caucasus of Abkhazia, a cave descends 2,212 metres below its entrance — the deepest known cave on Earth, surpassed in 2018 by another cave just down the mountain. Climbing down takes weeks; cavers camp in the cave for the descent. What is the cave called?
context: Cave depth is measured from highest entrance to lowest passage point. Krubera-Voronya was the world's deepest from 2001 to 2018; Veryovkina now holds the record at 2,212 m. Both lie in the Arabika Massif of Abkhazia.

question: In central Vietnam, a single cave passage measures 9 km long, with one section over 200 metres high and 150 metres wide — large enough that a Boeing 747 could fly through it. A jungle grows on the floor where sinkhole roofs have collapsed. What is the cave called?
context: Son Doong was only discovered by science in 1991 and first explored in 2009. The British Cave Research Association mapped it; tours started in 2013, limited to about 1,000 visitors per year. The cave has its own ecosystem of bats, river fish, and even monkeys living in the open sections.

question: Along tropical coastlines, salt-tolerant trees grow with their roots partly submerged in salty tidal water. Their tangled aerial root systems trap sediment, build land, and buffer storm surges. What is this kind of forest called?
context: Bangladesh's Sundarbans — the largest mangrove forest in the world — buffers Bangladesh from cyclonic surges. Mangrove loss accelerates storm damage; the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed disproportionately more people where mangroves had been cleared for shrimp farming. Restoration is a major coastal-engineering tool.

question: On Sicily's east coast rises Europe's largest active volcano — about 3,330 metres tall, although its summit height changes from eruption to eruption. UNESCO World Heritage 2013. The local Sicilian name for the mountain reflects the constancy of fire activity. What is the local nickname?
context: Etna has been continuously active for about 500,000 years. The Greek myth places the workshop of Hephaestus inside it. Etna's wine industry has revived in the past two decades — vineyards on lava-rich black soils.

question: On 27 August 1883, an Indonesian island volcano erupted in one of the most powerful explosions of modern recorded history. The sound was heard about 4,800 km away in Perth and Mauritius. The tsunami killed about 36,000 people. What is the volcano's name?
context: The 1883 eruption ejected about 21 cubic km of material. A new volcano — Anak Krakatau, 'Child of Krakatoa' — has been growing in the same caldera since 1927. A 2018 partial collapse of Anak Krakatau caused another deadly tsunami.

question: Beneath Yellowstone National Park sits one of the world's largest volcanic systems — a caldera 70 km across, formed by three colossal eruptions in the past 2.1 million years. The most recent (about 631,000 years ago) ejected about 1,000 cubic km of material. What kind of volcano is this?
context: Yellowstone's three giant eruptions came roughly 2.1, 1.3, and 0.63 million years ago — a rough 700,000-year interval. Whether the next one is geologically imminent or millions of years away is debated. The current state — geothermal features, slow uplift — is interpreted as 'active and restless'.

question: Around the Pacific Ocean basin runs a 40,000-km horseshoe-shaped belt that contains about 75% of the world's active and dormant volcanoes and about 90% of its earthquakes. The activity is driven by subduction at the basin's edges. What is this belt called?
context: Major Ring of Fire countries include Chile, Peru, Mexico, the U.S. (West Coast), Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, and New Zealand. Mount St Helens, Mount Pinatubo, Krakatoa, Tambora, Fuji, Mount Cotopaxi, and Popocatepetl are all on the ring.

question: Off the coasts of California, Chile, South Africa, and New Zealand, fast-growing brown algae form underwater 'forests' up to 50 metres tall. The species can grow 60 cm a day. Diverse species — sea otters, abalones, sheephead, leopard sharks — depend on them. What is the canopy-forming species along the U.S. West Coast?
context: Giant kelp anchors to rock with a holdfast, builds a stalk via internal gas-filled floats, and forms a canopy at the surface. Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins that otherwise overgraze the kelp; their return to California since the 1970s has restored vast kelp ecosystems.

question: Polynesian navigators settled the most remote islands on Earth — from Hawaii to Easter Island to New Zealand — between about 1000 BC and 1300 AD, sailing without maps, charts, sextants, or compasses. What suite of observational techniques did they use?
answer: Star compass, wave patterns, cloud signs, bird flight
choices: Star compass, wave patterns, cloud signs, bird flight
Solar elevation tables and lead-line soundings
Latitude beads carved on whale tooth implements
context: Mau Piailug of Satawal taught the lost art of Pacific wayfinding to Nainoa Thompson of the Hokule'a — a replica voyaging canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 using only traditional methods. The voyage proved that systematic deliberate navigation, not chance drift, settled the Pacific.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza, completed around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu, is aligned with the four cardinal directions to within about a tenth of a degree. The four sides of its base have lengths within a few centimetres of each other. About how many limestone blocks make it up?
context: Average block weight is about 2.5 tons; the largest in the King's Chamber weigh 50-80 tons. How they were moved and stacked is still debated; recently a papyrus of an overseer named Merer detailed limestone-block transport via canals. The pyramid's sides are oriented to within 3 arc minutes of cardinal directions.

question: Beside the Great Pyramid at Giza sits a colossal limestone statue of a recumbent lion with a human head — 73 metres long and 20 metres tall, carved from a single bedrock outcrop. The face is generally thought to portray Pharaoh Khafre (Khefren), Khufu's son. What is its English name?
context: The Sphinx has lost its nose — the popular story blaming Napoleon's troops is false; it was already gone in 18th-century drawings. Etched between its paws is the 'Dream Stele' of Thutmose IV (1400 BC), which describes a dream that led him to excavate the body from desert sand.

question: Beneath the western desert hills near Luxor lies a dry valley where most New Kingdom pharaohs (about 1500-1070 BC) were buried in rock-cut tombs. The 1922 discovery of one nearly intact royal tomb by Howard Carter (funded by Lord Carnarvon) made global headlines for years. Whose tomb was this?
context: Tutankhamun was a minor short-reigned pharaoh (1332-1323 BC), about 19 when he died. His tomb survived robbery because dust from cutting a later tomb above it concealed the entrance. Carter found over 5,000 objects, including the iconic gold death mask.

question: Inside the Great Temple of Amun at Karnak (modern Luxor) stretches the largest temple hall ever built — about 50 metres deep, 100 metres wide, supported by 134 sandstone columns up to 21 metres tall. Originally painted in vivid blues, reds, and yellows; reliefs cover every visible surface. What is this kind of column-filled hall called?
context: Pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II built most of the hall (around 1300-1280 BC). The central nave's tallest columns are larger than the supporting outer ranks; the height difference let clerestory windows admit light, dimly filtering down to the floor below. The columns are papyrus-bud and papyrus-flower shaped — a stone forest of the Nile marsh.

question: On the west bank of the Nile, four colossal seated statues of Pharaoh Ramesses II — each 20 metres tall — flank the entrance to a temple cut into the cliffside around 1264 BC. In the 1960s, the entire temple complex was cut into about 1,000 blocks (averaging 20 tons each) and moved to higher ground. Why?
answer: To save it from flooding by Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam
choices: To save it from flooding by Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam
To save it from earthquake damage in the Aswan area
To enable a new tourist-access tunnel for visitors
To consolidate it with the Karnak temple complex
context: The 1960-1968 rescue, funded by 50 countries through UNESCO, lifted the temple about 65 metres up and 200 metres back. Twice a year (22 February and 22 October), sunlight at dawn penetrates the inner sanctuary to illuminate the king and his deified self — the relocation preserved this within hours' difference.

question: The Nabataeans, who carved Petra into Jordanian sandstone cliffs from the 4th century BC onward, made the desert blossom by managing flash floods and rainfall. Their system of channels, cisterns, and dams stored enough water that Petra could host tens of thousands of people. What was the structure that diverted flash floods from the Siq?
choices: A buried channel from Wadi Araba
context: The flash floods in the Siq (the narrow canyon entrance) could and did kill visitors caught inside — 22 French tourists died in 1963 before the dam was repaired. The Nabataean channels around the cliffs and the dam at the canyon mouth kept the Siq dry through their 600-year occupation.

question: In central Syria stand the ruins of a Roman caravan city that briefly defied Rome under a warrior-queen in the 3rd century AD. Her armies captured Egypt and most of Anatolia before Emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272. Some of her temple and colonnade ruins were dynamited by ISIS in 2015. Who was the queen?
context: Zenobia (Septimia Bathzabbai Zenobia) claimed descent from Cleopatra. After her capture, accounts say she was paraded in golden chains through Rome, then either executed or settled to live as a Roman noblewoman. The ISIS destruction targeted the temples of Bel and Baalshamin and the Arch of Triumph.

question: In Lebanon's Bekaa Valley stand the ruins of one of the largest Roman temple complexes ever built, dedicated to Jupiter, Bacchus, and Venus in the 1st-3rd centuries AD. The Temple of Jupiter once had 54 columns; only six still stand. Foundation stones include some of the largest cut stones ever used. About how heavy is the largest?
context: The 'Stone of the Pregnant Woman' in a nearby quarry was never moved; a similar 1,650-ton stone was found there in 2014. How the Romans moved similar (smaller) stones to Baalbek's foundations is unclear. The site predates Roman use — it had been sacred for millennia.

question: Founded by Darius the Great around 515 BC in southern Iran, the ceremonial capital of the Persian Achaemenid Empire featured a vast audience hall (the Apadana) reached by long stairs whose carved reliefs depict envoys from 23 subject nations bringing tribute. Each envoy is shown in his own national dress. What kind of stone are the reliefs carved into?
answer: Limestone (grey limestone of the local quarries)
choices: Limestone (grey limestone of the local quarries)
context: Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC; whether as a deliberate revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens or in a drunken party is debated. The relief programme — about 3,000 figures — survives because limestone resists weathering in the dry climate. UNESCO World Heritage 1979.

question: About 90 km northeast of Persepolis stands the simple six-stepped limestone tomb of the founder of the Persian Empire, who died around 530 BC after building the largest empire the world had yet seen. Alexander the Great paid his respects there in 324 BC. Whose tomb is this?
context: The tomb is a 6-metre-tall house-shaped chamber on a stepped platform. Cyrus's empire stretched from Anatolia to Central Asia; he is praised in the Hebrew Bible for freeing the Jews from Babylonian captivity. The Cyrus Cylinder (a clay barrel with his proclamation) is sometimes called the first declaration of human rights.

question: In southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), one of the earliest cities of human civilisation rose around 4000 BC. By 2100 BC, King Ur-Nammu built a vast three-tier brick stepped temple platform here. The kingdom of Ur was the home of the biblical Abraham. What kind of structure is the stepped temple platform called?
context: Ziggurat means 'raised up' or 'high' in Akkadian. The Ziggurat of Ur is one of the best-preserved; American 20th-century reconstruction restored the lowest tier. Ziggurats were not tombs but temple platforms — the shrine of the god sat at the top. The biblical Tower of Babel is thought to be inspired by the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon.

question: The eighth gate to the inner city of ancient Babylon was built around 575 BC under Nebuchadnezzar II — its surface entirely covered in glazed blue bricks with relief figures of dragons (mushhushshu) and bulls. The gate was excavated by German archaeologists in 1902-1914 and reassembled in a museum. Where does it stand today?
context: Only the smaller front section was reconstructed in Berlin; the rest sits in storage. A reproduction stands at the original Babylon site in Iraq. Iraq has periodically demanded the return of the gate; Germany has not complied. The Ishtar Gate's blue is from glazes coloured by ground lapis lazuli.

question: The mythical site of Homer's Iliad was found in 1870-90 by the German amateur Heinrich Schliemann digging at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey. Schliemann found that the site contained multiple superimposed cities — at least nine, going back to the Bronze Age. How did Schliemann's digging methods damage the site?
answer: He dug a deep trench through to bedrock, destroying upper layers
choices: He dug a deep trench through to bedrock, destroying upper layers
He used explosives that destroyed key foundations
He removed all artefacts to Russia in unmarked boxes
He left the trenches open, exposing the ruins to weather damage
context: Schliemann's 'Troy II' (a Bronze Age city he had identified with Homer's Troy) actually predates the Trojan War by a thousand years. The true Homeric layer is now identified as Troy VIIa, which was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC — close to traditional dating.

question: On a hill in Greece's Peloponnese stand the ruins of one of the major Bronze Age citadel-cities of the Aegean. Its main entrance is topped by a massive triangular relief of two heraldic lions flanking a central column — one of the oldest sculptural monuments in Europe (around 1250 BC). What is this gate called?
context: The lions' heads are missing — they may have been made of separate inset stones. The walls of Mycenae are built of stones so large the later Greeks thought only Cyclopes could have moved them; 'Cyclopean masonry' is the technical term. Heinrich Schliemann also dug Mycenae; he found a gold death mask he called 'the mask of Agamemnon'.

question: On the island of Crete, the largest Bronze Age palace in Greece was excavated 1900-1931 by Sir Arthur Evans. He named the civilisation after the legendary king Minos. The complex's many corridors and rooms (over 1,000) probably inspired the Greek myth of a particular monster's lair. What was the monster?
context: Evans was a controversial figure; he heavily reconstructed Knossos in concrete, which most modern archaeologists consider too speculative. The Minoan script Linear A remains undeciphered; Linear B was cracked in 1952 by Michael Ventris and proved to be an early form of Greek.

question: On the Greek Peloponnese, an open-air theatre built around 340 BC seats 14,000 spectators on stone benches climbing a hillside. Its acoustics are famous: a coin dropped at the centre stage can be heard in the back row, 60 metres away. The shape and gradient are responsible. What is this theatre called?
context: Recent acoustic research credits the stone steps acting as a corrugated filter — they let high frequencies (consonants and the higher partials of vowels) through to the rear seats while dampening low background noise. The theatre is part of the Sanctuary of Asclepius, the ancient Greek god of medicine.

question: At Olympia in Greece, the ancient sanctuary of Zeus held a 12-metre seated statue of the god — gold and ivory over a wooden core, designed by Phidias around 435 BC. It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. What happened to the statue?
answer: It was moved to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire around 475 AD
choices: It was moved to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire around 475 AD
It was buried beneath the Olympia temple ruins and never recovered
It was shipped to Rome and was lost when Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii
It still survives, in the Olympia archaeological museum
context: After Christianity replaced classical religion, the statue lost its function. Theodosius II moved it to Constantinople in the 4th century; it perished in the great Lauseion palace fire. The Olympia temple itself was destroyed by earthquakes in the 5th-6th centuries. The site hosted the ancient Olympic Games from about 776 BC.

question: On the Aegean coast of Anatolia (modern Bergama, Turkey), a great altar to Zeus was built around 175 BC by the Pergamene kingdom. Its monumental friezes depict the Gigantomachy — the battle between gods and giants — in some of the most dynamic Hellenistic sculpture ever carved. Where is the main altar today?
context: Sourced as part of late-19th-century German excavations and shipped to Berlin between 1879 and 1886. Turkey periodically requests its return. The Gigantomachy frieze is about 113 metres long — one of the longest surviving sculptural narratives from antiquity.

question: At Ephesus in western Anatolia, a Roman library facade — twin storeys of paired columns and four statue niches representing wisdom, knowledge, intelligence, and virtue — has been reconstructed from the ruins. Once it held about 12,000 scrolls. After whom was the library named?
