context: The Red Fort houses the Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience), Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audience), and the marble Naubat Khana. The Indian prime minister addresses the nation from the Red Fort's main gate every Independence Day.

question: Along the western bank of the Ganges river in the north Indian city of Varanasi (Kashi, Banaras), more than 80 stone-stepped ghats descend into the river. Two of these ghats are reserved for a particular religious purpose. What is it?
answer: Open-air Hindu cremation — Manikarnika Ghat and Harishchandra Ghat are continuous-burning cremation grounds
choices: Open-air Hindu cremation — Manikarnika Ghat and Harishchandra Ghat are continuous-burning cremation grounds
Open-air Hindu marriages — both ghats are sacred sites for traditional Brahmin wedding ceremonies
Open-air Shaivite initiations — both ghats hold three-day initiation rituals for new Hindu monks
Open-air Muslim ablutions — both ghats are accessible to the city's Muslim community for prayer washing
context: Dying in Varanasi is held in Hindu tradition to bring moksha (release from rebirth). The cremation ghats burn around the clock; family members bring the body to the river, cremate it, and consign the ashes to the Ganges.

question: Each weekday morning in Mumbai, a group of roughly 5,000 deliverymen pick up freshly cooked lunch boxes from suburban homes, ride trains into central Mumbai, deliver them to office workers by midday, then return the empty containers in the afternoon. The system handles around 200,000 lunches a day. What is the error rate of this system?
answer: About one mistake in every six million deliveries — Six Sigma quality with no computer tracking
choices: About one mistake in every six million deliveries — Six Sigma quality with no computer tracking
About one mistake in every six thousand deliveries — comparable to a normal urban courier service
About one mistake in every six hundred deliveries — common enough that diners check each box
About one mistake in every sixty deliveries — the system relies on luck more than coordination
context: The dabbawalas' lunch-boxes ('dabbas') use a simple coded marking system instead of barcodes or apps. Forbes and Harvard Business School have written case studies on the dabbawala system as an example of low-tech operational excellence.

question: The walled old city of Jaipur in Rajasthan, northern India, is painted entirely in a uniform pink-orange terracotta hue — by city ordinance, every building inside the walls keeps the same colour. The convention dates to a single 19th-century event. What was it?
answer: Maharaja Ram Singh ordered the city painted pink in 1876 to welcome Edward, Prince of Wales, on his Indian tour
choices: Maharaja Ram Singh ordered the city painted pink in 1876 to welcome Edward, Prince of Wales, on his Indian tour
Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II decreed the colour at the city's founding in 1727 to honour the Rajput warrior caste
Maharaja Madho Singh II repainted the city in 1922 to celebrate the visit of King George V to Delhi
The British viceroy Lord Curzon ordered Jaipur painted pink in 1903 to mark the Coronation Durbar that year
context: Jaipur was the first planned city in Mughal-era India, laid out on a nine-block grid by Sawai Jai Singh II in 1727. The 1876 paint decree stuck; the city has been formally the 'Pink City' since.

question: In central Jaipur stands a small park containing 19 large stone astronomical instruments built between 1727 and 1734 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II. One of them — a triangle of stone rising 27 meters tall — is the largest stone sundial in the world. What does this instrument measure?
answer: Time, accurate to about two seconds — by the shadow of its hypotenuse falling across two graduated quadrants
choices: Time, accurate to about two seconds — by the shadow of its hypotenuse falling across two graduated quadrants
The position of Polaris, north of the celestial pole — by sightlines along the slanting hypotenuse
The summer-solstice azimuth of sunrise on the local horizon — by the orientation of its base
The latitude of Jaipur, to a fraction of a degree — by the angle of the structure's central wall
context: The 'Vrihat Samrat Yantra' (Great Sundial) is still accurate today; its shadow moves at the visible speed of about a meter every five minutes. Sawai Jai Singh built four other Jantar Mantars across northern India to verify each other's observations.

question: The ruins of Ayutthaya, the historic Thai capital sacked by the Burmese in 1767, lie north of modern Bangkok. Among the most photographed images of Thailand is a stone Buddha head from one of Ayutthaya's temples — Wat Phra Mahathat — embedded in the roots of which tree?
answer: A bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa), whose growing roots gradually wrapped around the broken stone head
choices: A bodhi tree (Ficus religiosa), whose growing roots gradually wrapped around the broken stone head
A teak tree, the prized hardwood once dominant in central Thai forests
A baobab tree, planted in Ayutthaya by 17th-century European traders for ornamental reasons
A mango tree, native to the lower Chao Phraya river valley around Ayutthaya
context: The bodhi tree is the same species under which the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. Modern conservation rules require visitors at Wat Phra Mahathat to be lower than the head when photographing it, out of respect.

question: On the east bank of the Chao Phraya river in central Bangkok rises a walled complex of pavilions, golden chedis, and lacquered roofs — the Thai royal palace begun in 1782 when the new Chakri dynasty moved the capital from Thonburi. Inside one chapel sits a small dark-green jade statue, the most venerated image in Thailand. What is this image called?
answer: The Emerald Buddha (Phra Kaew Morakot), a jade or jasper statue dressed in seasonal gold costumes by the king
choices: The Emerald Buddha (Phra Kaew Morakot), a jade or jasper statue dressed in seasonal gold costumes by the king
The Smiling Buddha, a 12th-century stone Khmer image from the temples of Lopburi
The Walking Buddha, the elegant elongated bronze stride image specific to Sukhothai-era sculpture
The Reclining Buddha, the gilded 46-meter image actually housed at Wat Pho nearby
context: The Emerald Buddha probably dates from the 15th century; its origin is disputed (Chiang Rai, Vientiane, Cambodia). The Thai king himself, in person, changes its golden robes three times a year to mark the Thai seasons.

question: Adjacent to Bangkok's Grand Palace is one of the oldest Buddhist temples in the city, founded under King Rama I and famous for a single immense gilded image. The image is 46 meters long and 15 meters tall and reclines on its right side with its head supported on its right hand. What is this temple called?
answer: Wat Pho (Wat Phra Chetuphon), traditionally the birthplace of Thai massage
choices: Wat Pho (Wat Phra Chetuphon), traditionally the birthplace of Thai massage
Wat Arun, the riverside 'Temple of Dawn' with its tall central prang
Wat Saket, the 'Golden Mount' rising from a small artificial hill in central Bangkok
Wat Mahathat, a 14th-century royal temple at the edge of the Sanam Luang ceremonial ground
context: Wat Pho is famous as the founding teaching site of traditional Thai massage. The reclining Buddha depicts Sakyamuni at the moment of parinirvana (final passing). The temple's grounds also hold 91 chedis of varying size.

question: About 50 km north of Seoul, South Korea's capital, lies a 4-km-wide buffer strip extending 250 km coast to coast across the Korean peninsula. The strip has been almost untouched by people since 1953. What unintended consequence has this had?
answer: The strip has become one of the most biodiverse temperate ecosystems in Asia, with cranes, deer, and rare leopards
choices: The strip has become one of the most biodiverse temperate ecosystems in Asia, with cranes, deer, and rare leopards
The strip has become permanently radioactive due to leaching from nearby Korean nuclear test sites
The strip has become a major Russian-Chinese commercial trade corridor under a 1990s exemption
The strip has been gradually returned to North Korean control under a series of small UN agreements
context: The DMZ shelters rare red-crowned cranes, Asiatic black bears, and possibly Amur leopards. Both Koreas remain technically at war — only an armistice was signed in 1953, not a peace treaty. The Joint Security Area at Panmunjom is the only place where opposing soldiers stand face to face.

question: About 6 km from the modern Cambodian town of Siem Reap lie the vast 9th-12th-century ruins of an empire's capital — temples, reservoirs, ceremonial roads, and the famous moat-and-temple complex covering nearly 400 sq km. Which empire built this complex?
answer: The Khmer Empire under successive god-kings, with Suryavarman II building Angkor Wat itself around 1113-1150
choices: The Khmer Empire under successive god-kings, with Suryavarman II building Angkor Wat itself around 1113-1150
The Champa kingdom of central Vietnam, which controlled the Cambodian lowlands for several centuries
The Sukhothai kingdom of north-central Thailand, which absorbed Angkor in the late 13th century
The Tang Chinese dynasty, which administered Indochina through tributary appointments
context: The Khmer Empire dominated mainland Southeast Asia for roughly 500 years; Angkor was its capital. The complex was 'lost' to the West until French explorers publicised it in the 1860s, though locals had always known it.

question: On the eastern bank of the Irrawaddy river in central Myanmar lies a plain on which roughly 2,200 Buddhist temples, pagodas, and monastic ruins still stand — built between the 11th and 13th centuries under a Burmese kingdom. What was this kingdom?
answer: The Pagan Kingdom (also spelled Bagan), the first major Burmese state, ruling roughly 1044-1287
choices: The Pagan Kingdom (also spelled Bagan), the first major Burmese state, ruling roughly 1044-1287
The Toungoo dynasty, a later 16th-century Burmese state ruling from a different capital
The Konbaung dynasty, the late-18th-century Burmese state that fought three wars with British India
The Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy, based at Bago in lower Burma and rivalling Bagan
context: Bagan's temple-building came to a near-stop after Kublai Khan's Mongol invasion in the late 13th century. The site was a UNESCO World Heritage candidate denied for decades, finally inscribed in 2019 after restoration controversies.

question: On a hill above central Yangon (Rangoon), Myanmar, rises a 99-meter gilded stupa — the Shwedagon Pagoda. Pilgrims walk barefoot around its broad marble terrace, past hundreds of smaller shrines. The stupa's spire is plated in solid gold and topped with diamonds. According to Buddhist tradition, what does the central stupa enshrine?
answer: Eight strands of hair given by the Buddha himself to two merchant brothers from Burma
choices: Eight strands of hair given by the Buddha himself to two merchant brothers from Burma
The Buddha's right tooth, given to a king of medieval Burma by Sri Lankan Buddhist envoys
A finger bone of the Buddha's foremost disciple Sariputta, brought to Burma in the 5th century AD
A 17th-century carved wooden Buddha image from the Bagan-era court workshops upriver
context: The two merchants, Taphussa and Bhallika, are said to have met the Buddha shortly after his enlightenment. The Shwedagon's gold plating is regularly renewed; the diamond bud at the very top is set with thousands of stones.

question: The Singapore skyline includes the Marina Bay Sands resort — three 55-story towers joined at the top by a long horizontal SkyPark with an infinity-edge swimming pool. The entire Marina Bay district sits on land that did not exist a century ago. How did it appear?
answer: Through land reclamation — sand dredged from the seabed and from offshore islands, raising the bay floor above sea level
choices: Through land reclamation — sand dredged from the seabed and from offshore islands, raising the bay floor above sea level
Through subsidence inversion — the original 1850s Singapore seabed rose during 20th-century tectonic adjustment
Through harbor draining — colonial engineers pumped out a small back bay and built the new district on its floor
Through coral growth — the bay had filled naturally with coral until the seabed reached the high-tide line
context: Singapore has expanded its land area by roughly 25% through reclamation since independence in 1965. Marina Bay was created on reclaimed seabed; Jurong, Tuas, and Changi are similarly built on dredged land. Sand imports are politically sensitive across Southeast Asia.

question: In central Java, Indonesia, a 9th-century Buddhist temple of stepped terraces rises out of the rice paddies. Pilgrims walk up six square terraces and three round terraces, ending at a great central stupa surrounded by 72 perforated bell-shaped stupas, each containing a Buddha statue. What is this monument called?
answer: Borobudur, the largest single Buddhist monument in the world, built under the Sailendra dynasty around 800 AD
choices: Borobudur, the largest single Buddhist monument in the world, built under the Sailendra dynasty around 800 AD
Prambanan, the major Hindu temple complex nearby, dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva
Plaosan, the dual Buddhist-Hindu temple complex east of Yogyakarta
Ratu Boko, the small ruined royal complex on the hill south of Prambanan
context: Borobudur is shaped as a mandala. Each terrace level represents a stage of Buddhist cosmology, from kama-dhatu (desire) at the base through rupa-dhatu (form) to arupa-dhatu (formless) at the summit. The monument was effectively abandoned after the 10th century and rediscovered by Raffles in 1814.

question: About 50 km east of Yogyakarta on Java stands a 9th-century Hindu temple complex of soaring slender tower-shrines — over 240 individual structures originally, organised around three central temples for Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. The tallest central shrine reaches 47 meters. What is this complex called?
answer: Prambanan, the largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia and a UNESCO heritage site
choices: Prambanan, the largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia and a UNESCO heritage site
Borobudur, the larger Buddhist stupa complex on the western side of the same fertile plain
Pura Besakih, the mother temple of Hinduism on the island of Bali
Tampaksiring, a small Balinese spring-and-temple complex at the centre of the island
context: Prambanan was built by the Sanjaya dynasty in roughly the same century the Sailendras were building Borobudur. The Indonesian shadow-puppet performances enact the Ramayana on its grounds during major festivals.

question: On the southwestern tip of the island of Bali in Indonesia, a small Balinese Hindu temple sits at the edge of a 70-meter cliff that drops straight to the Indian Ocean. The temple is one of six 'kayangan jagad' (directional temples) that protect the island. What is this temple called?
answer: Pura Luhur Uluwatu, one of Bali's nine directional temples and home to a famous evening kecak dance performance
choices: Pura Luhur Uluwatu, one of Bali's nine directional temples and home to a famous evening kecak dance performance
Pura Besakih, the 'mother temple' on the slopes of Mount Agung in eastern Bali
Pura Tanah Lot, the smaller cliff temple in the west, accessible at low tide on a basalt sea stack
Pura Ulun Danu Bratan, the temple complex on the central crater lake of Bali
context: Pura Tanah Lot is also dramatic but smaller and on a sea stack. Pura Luhur Uluwatu has monkeys on its grounds and hosts the evening kecak dance — a chorus of men chanting 'cak-cak-cak' under the sunset over the ocean.

question: The old quarter of Hanoi, Vietnam, north of Hoan Kiem Lake, is a dense network of narrow streets named for the goods that craft guilds once traded in each one — silver, silk, paper, sugar, basket-weaving, bamboo. By tradition, how many such streets are there?
answer: Thirty-six (the '36 streets,' though the modern quarter has more than the traditional count)
choices: Thirty-six (the '36 streets,' though the modern quarter has more than the traditional count)
Seventy-two — twice the traditional count, organised in two concentric rings around the inner core
One hundred eight — a Buddhist sacred number adopted by the city in the medieval period
Twenty-four — one street per hour of the day in classical Vietnamese tradition
context: Each guild had its protective patron saint and its own communal house. The pattern reflects Hanoi's pre-modern role as the major artisan-trading capital of the Red River delta; many streets still sell something close to their original goods.

question: Each morning around dawn in the small Laotian city of Luang Prabang, hundreds of saffron-robed monks walk in single-file procession through the streets, accepting rice and small offerings from kneeling lay donors. The ceremony is one of the most photographed in Southeast Asia. What is it called?
answer: Tak Bat, the Theravada Buddhist tradition of daily alms-giving by the laity to monks
choices: Tak Bat, the Theravada Buddhist tradition of daily alms-giving by the laity to monks
Songkran, the traditional Buddhist New Year water-throwing festival in mid-April
Vesak, the Buddhist commemoration of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and death
Loi Krathong, the river-lantern festival of the Lao and Thai November full moon
context: Tak Bat happens daily across Theravada-Buddhist countries (Laos, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Sri Lanka) but Luang Prabang is famous for the scale and visual concentration of the procession through its historic main street.

question: In central Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, rise two 88-story stainless-steel-and-glass towers, connected at the 41st and 42nd floors by a sky bridge. The towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004. What is unusual about their geometric ground plan?
answer: Each tower's floor plate is a stylised eight-pointed Islamic star, evoking traditional geometric patterns
choices: Each tower's floor plate is a stylised eight-pointed Islamic star, evoking traditional geometric patterns
Each tower's floor plate is a perfect circle, the first round high-rise structure of its scale on Earth
Each tower's floor plate is a hexagon, modelled on the Malaysian Bunga Raya (hibiscus) flower of state
Each tower's floor plate is a stylised Chinese yin-yang symbol, reflecting Malaysia's plural culture
context: The Petronas Towers' Rub el Hizb octagram floor plan was designed by Cesar Pelli with Malaysian Islamic patrons. They lost the 'tallest' crown to Taipei 101 (2004) and then to the Burj Khalifa (2010).

question: The medieval Florentine poet Dante Alighieri began writing his Divine Comedy around 1308, while in political exile from his home city. The poem opens 'midway in the journey of our life' as Dante finds himself in a dark wood and is guided through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. Who guides him through Hell and most of Purgatory?
answer: The Roman poet Virgil, author of the Aeneid, sent to him as a guide from the spirit of his beloved Beatrice
choices: The Roman poet Virgil, author of the Aeneid, sent to him as a guide from the spirit of his beloved Beatrice
The Greek poet Homer, author of the Iliad, accompanied by the Roman historian Livy as a second guide
The Roman emperor Augustus, who shows Dante the political ruin of late medieval Italy
The apostle Peter, sent down from heaven explicitly to escort him through the lower realms
context: Beatrice (the real-life Beatrice Portinari) guides Dante through Paradise. Dante shaped Italian into a national literary language; his Florentine Tuscan became the basis for modern standard Italian.

question: From around the year 1000 to 1797, the Most Serene Republic of Venice was ruled by an elected Doge ('Duke'). The election process was famously baroque: a series of randomised reductions and votes designed to prevent any one family from gaming the system. How many separate stages did the Doge's election ultimately go through?
answer: Ten stages — alternating lottery and ballot — designed to dilute factional influence among the noble families
choices: Ten stages — alternating lottery and ballot — designed to dilute factional influence among the noble families
Three stages — quick succession of votes in the Great Council, the Senate, and the College — designed for speed
Twenty stages — one for each year of typical Doge tenure — designed to express the duration of office in process
Forty stages — one for each noble family eligible to provide a Doge — designed to give each clan equal voice
context: The process limited Venetian dynasties but produced doges through extreme old age — the office was for life. By the 18th century Venice had ossified into a museum of itself; Napoleon ended the republic in 1797.

question: In 490 BC the Athenian army defeated a much larger Persian invasion force on the plain of Marathon, north of the city. Tradition says a messenger ran the distance back to Athens to bring news of the victory, gasped 'Nenikekamen!' ('We have won!'), and dropped dead. What modern athletic event commemorates this run?
answer: The marathon race, run at 42.195 km — fixed at this length for the 1908 London Olympics
choices: The marathon race, run at 42.195 km — fixed at this length for the 1908 London Olympics
The decathlon, a ten-event athletics competition that closes every modern Olympic Games
The pentathlon, modelled directly on the five-event ancient Greek Olympic original
The triathlon, a swim-bike-run race combining the three forms of ancient Greek movement training
context: The original course at the 1896 Athens Olympics ran roughly the actual Marathon-to-Athens distance, about 40 km. The 1908 London course was extended so the royal family could watch the finish from Windsor Castle.

question: Ancient Rome was traditionally said to be built on seven hills inside its early walls: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal, and Viminal. The hills themselves were the basis of the early city's defensive strength and ritual geography. What did the Romans tradition say happened on one of these hills, the Palatine, in 753 BC?
answer: Romulus founded the city after killing his brother Remus in a dispute over which of the seven hills to settle
choices: Romulus founded the city after killing his brother Remus in a dispute over which of the seven hills to settle
Aeneas landed there as a refugee from the sack of Troy and founded the original village of Roma
The Etruscan king Tarquinius drove out the Latins and built the first defensive walls around the seven hills
Lucius Junius Brutus established the Roman Republic, on the date later commemorated as the founding day
context: Roman emperors built their palaces on the Palatine (hence the word 'palace'). The Aventine was plebeian, the Capitoline was civic-religious; each hill had its own ritual associations through the imperial period.

question: The dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, rising 136 meters above the basilica floor, was designed by Michelangelo in his last years and completed after his death in the 1590s. Whose work was Michelangelo's dome consciously responding to?
answer: Filippo Brunelleschi, whose 1436 dome over Florence Cathedral set the model for the Renaissance large-span dome
choices: Filippo Brunelleschi, whose 1436 dome over Florence Cathedral set the model for the Renaissance large-span dome
Christopher Wren, whose later 1675 design for St. Paul's Cathedral in London influenced Roman dome practice
Hadrian's Pantheon, whose 2nd-century concrete dome remained the largest in the world during Michelangelo's life
Justinian's Hagia Sophia, whose 6th-century Byzantine dome introduced pendentive geometry to Renaissance architects
context: Brunelleschi's Florence dome was the explicit precedent; Michelangelo even said his St. Peter's dome would be 'larger but not more beautiful' than his predecessor's. St. Peter's dome can be climbed and offers a famous view of Rome.

question: In an apartment at Berggasse 19 in Vienna, between roughly 1891 and 1938, a neurologist treated patients on a couch by inviting them to free-associate while he listened from a chair just behind. He gradually developed the doctrine that adult neurosis arose from repressed childhood material — and that dreams encoded that material in disguise. Who was he?
answer: Sigmund Freud, founder of psychoanalysis, who fled Vienna for London in 1938 after the Nazi annexation
choices: Sigmund Freud, founder of psychoanalysis, who fled Vienna for London in 1938 after the Nazi annexation
Carl Jung, founder of analytical psychology, who worked alongside Freud in Vienna before breaking with him
Alfred Adler, founder of individual psychology, who served as Freud's deputy president of the Vienna society
Wilhelm Stekel, an early Viennese disciple of Freud who later broke with him over methods of dream interpretation
context: Jung and Adler were collaborators who broke with Freud over theory. The Berggasse 19 apartment is now the Sigmund Freud Museum; Freud died in London in 1939 from advanced cancer of the jaw.

question: On the outskirts of Vienna stands the yellow Habsburg summer palace of Schonbrunn, completed in the 1740s under the empress Maria Theresa. The palace has 1,441 rooms, of which 40 are open to visitors. It was the principal scene of Maria Theresa's family life; she bore 16 children there. Who was the most famous of those children?
answer: Marie Antoinette, last queen of France, executed in Paris in 1793 after the fall of the monarchy
choices: Marie Antoinette, last queen of France, executed in Paris in 1793 after the fall of the monarchy
Sissi (Empress Elisabeth of Austria), wife of Franz Joseph, who lived a century later than Maria Theresa
Maria Stuarda (Mary Queen of Scots), a Catholic queen who actually lived two centuries earlier
Catherine the Great of Russia, who was unrelated to the Habsburgs but ruled in the same era
context: Sissi was Franz Joseph's wife (1854); both Sissi and Maria Theresa were strongly associated with Schonbrunn but a century apart. Mozart played at Schonbrunn at age six, in 1762, before the empress and her children.

question: The Upper Belvedere palace in Vienna, built for Prince Eugene of Savoy in 1722, today houses Austria's largest collection of Gustav Klimt — including the painting that has become Vienna's modern visual icon: a couple embracing on a flowering meadow, both figures wrapped in cascading gold leaf squares and spirals. What is this painting called?
answer: The Kiss (Der Kuss), painted by Klimt around 1907-1908 during his 'golden phase' of decorated panels
choices: The Kiss (Der Kuss), painted by Klimt around 1907-1908 during his 'golden phase' of decorated panels
The Embrace (Die Umarmung), the alternate German title for Klimt's earlier Adele Bloch-Bauer I portrait
The Tree of Life (Lebensbaum), painted by Klimt for the Stoclet Frieze in Brussels in the same years
The Lovers (Die Liebenden), a smaller and lesser-known Klimt panel that hangs in the Leopold Museum in Vienna
context: Klimt's Kiss is one of the most-reproduced paintings of the early 20th century. Adele Bloch-Bauer I, restituted to her heirs in 2006 and sold to Ronald Lauder for $135 million, hangs at the Neue Galerie in New York.

question: Behind a movable bookcase in a 17th-century canal-side house at Prinsengracht 263 in Amsterdam, a Jewish family hid for over two years during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. The teenage daughter kept a diary that has been translated into more than 70 languages. Who was she, and how did the world come to know her diary?
answer: Anne Frank, whose father Otto — the only survivor of the family — found her diary after the war and arranged its 1947 publication
choices: Anne Frank, whose father Otto — the only survivor of the family — found her diary after the war and arranged its 1947 publication
Hannah Goslar, Anne's friend, whose diary the Frank family helped preserve while in hiding behind the bookcase
Edith Frank, Anne's mother, who recorded the family's daily life until her deportation to Auschwitz in 1944
Margot Frank, Anne's older sister, whose unfinished memoir was completed by Otto Frank after the war
context: Anne died at Bergen-Belsen in early 1945. The Frank house opened as a museum in 1960; the original red-checked diary is still on display, behind glass, in the rooms where it was written.

question: On the Pariser Platz in central Berlin stands a sandstone neoclassical city gate built in 1788-1791 — six fluted Doric columns supporting a horizontal entablature, topped by a copper-green chariot of Victory with four horses. During the Cold War the gate stood in the Soviet sector of Berlin, with the Wall running just past it. What is the gate called?
answer: The Brandenburg Gate (Brandenburger Tor), modelled on the Propylaea of the Athenian Acropolis
choices: The Brandenburg Gate (Brandenburger Tor), modelled on the Propylaea of the Athenian Acropolis
The Reichstag Gate, named for the German parliament building visible behind it through 19th-century photographs
The Charlottenburg Gate, named for the western Berlin palace district reachable through it via the Tiergarten
The Spandau Gate, named for the small western district that lies on the road continuing through the gate westward
context: Carl Gotthard Langhans designed the gate; Johann Gottfried Schadow added the Quadriga statue. Napoleon stole the Quadriga to Paris in 1806; the Prussians took it back in 1814. The reopening of the gate in 1989 was the symbolic moment of German reunification.

question: On the western shore of the bay of Havana in Cuba sits a 16th-century walled city whose old plazas, baroque churches, colonial palaces, and pastel townhouses earned UNESCO inscription in 1982. The city was founded by which power, and when?
answer: By Spain in 1519, after the city was moved to its current site to face the Gulf of Mexico's trade winds
choices: By Spain in 1519, after the city was moved to its current site to face the Gulf of Mexico's trade winds
By Spain in 1574, after replacing an older Taino settlement abandoned during the 1530s sugar boom
By France in 1665, when Louis XIV briefly held the western half of the Cuban coastline
By Britain in 1762, during the year-long Royal Navy occupation of Havana as part of the Seven Years' War
context: Havana became the principal Spanish New World port: silver fleets from Mexico and South America gathered here for the convoy run home. The British captured Havana in 1762 but returned it to Spain a year later in exchange for Florida.

question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast lies a walled colonial city whose 11 km of stone fortifications and outlying forts made it the most heavily defended Spanish harbour in the New World. Spanish silver gathered here for the trans-Atlantic fleet. What was the most famous unsuccessful siege of the city?
answer: The 1741 British siege under Admiral Edward Vernon — repulsed by yellow fever and a small Spanish garrison under Blas de Lezo
choices: The 1741 British siege under Admiral Edward Vernon — repulsed by yellow fever and a small Spanish garrison under Blas de Lezo
The 1586 English raid under Francis Drake — Drake captured and ransomed the city but withdrew
The 1697 French raid under Bernard de Pointis — France held Cartagena briefly before withdrawing
The 1819 republican siege under Simon Bolivar — Bolivar took the city ending Spanish rule
context: Drake actually did raid Cartagena in 1586. Vernon's 1741 siege was the great failure — over 18,000 British and colonial troops attacked but were defeated by tropical disease and Blas de Lezo's 3,000-man garrison. Cartagena's UNESCO walls remain almost entirely intact.

question: The Ecuadorian capital lies in a long narrow Andean valley at 2,850 meters — making it the second-highest national capital in the world. Its colonial old town, the largest and least-altered in the Americas, was the first UNESCO World Heritage Site. What was the local pre-Columbian power before the Spanish?
answer: The Inca Empire, which incorporated the highland kingdom of Quito under Huayna Capac in the late 15th century
choices: The Inca Empire, which incorporated the highland kingdom of Quito under Huayna Capac in the late 15th century
The Aztec Empire, which extended its tributary network into northwestern South America by 1500
The Tiwanaku Empire, the Bolivian-Peruvian highland power that absorbed Quito by 800 AD
The Chibcha Confederation, a Colombian-highland federation that briefly held the Quito basin
context: Quito was the second Inca capital under Huayna Capac, whose two heirs Atahualpa and Huascar split the empire and fought a civil war just before Pizarro arrived. La Paz, Bolivia, is higher (de facto capital), making Quito the second-highest national capital.

question: In the Andean highlands of Peru, at 3,400 meters, sits a city whose Quechua name means 'navel of the world.' The Inca built it on the model of a puma — the great central plaza forming the puma's body, the fortress of Sacsayhuaman its head. Who finally captured the city for Spain?
answer: Francisco Pizarro and his force of fewer than 200 Spaniards in November 1533
choices: Francisco Pizarro and his force of fewer than 200 Spaniards in November 1533
Hernan Cortes, fresh from his conquest of Mexico, leading the southern expansion of New Spain
Diego de Almagro, who marched independently from Panama to seize Cusco from Pizarro
Pedro de Alvarado, after his abortive Guatemalan-Ecuadorian campaign in the 1530s
context: Pizarro had captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca a year before, executing him after collecting a famous room-full of gold as ransom. Spain's seizure of Cusco effectively ended the Inca Empire, though Inca resistance continued at Vilcabamba until 1572.

question: On a hilltop above the Inca capital of Cusco in Peru, three terraced lines of dry-stone wall stretch in zig-zag formation. Each wall is built of massive polygonal limestone blocks fitted together without mortar so precisely that a knife blade cannot fit between them. The largest block weighs around 125 tonnes. What is this site called?
answer: Sacsayhuaman, the Inca fortress-temple complex above Cusco — also the head of the puma-shaped city
choices: Sacsayhuaman, the Inca fortress-temple complex above Cusco — also the head of the puma-shaped city
Coricancha, the gold-clad Sun Temple in central Cusco beneath the Spanish church of Santo Domingo
Pisac, the terraced agricultural and ritual complex above the Urubamba river east of Cusco
Ollantaytambo, the terraced fortress-town in the Sacred Valley downriver from Cusco
context: The Spanish dismantled much of Sacsayhuaman for building stone in colonial Cusco. The largest stones were too heavy to move and remain in place. Inca stoneworking technique — how it was achieved without iron tools — is still debated.

question: The modern city of Lima, Peru, is built over multiple ancient pyramid-platforms — adobe mounds that predate the Spanish founding of the city in 1535 by a thousand years or more. Many sit awkwardly inside modern neighbourhoods like Miraflores. What are these structures called locally?
answer: Huacas — sacred mounds and platforms built by the pre-Inca Lima and Ychsma cultures of the Peruvian coast
choices: Huacas — sacred mounds and platforms built by the pre-Inca Lima and Ychsma cultures of the Peruvian coast
Tepes — the dust-mound equivalent of Iranian archaeology, used here in a Quechua loan-translation
Cuevas — limestone caves modified into burial platforms by the coastal cultures of central Peru
Ushnus — small Inca-period altar-platforms built across the empire, usually paired with rectangular plazas
context: Huaca Pucllana in Miraflores is the most-visited; Huaca Huallamarca in San Isidro is another. The Lima and Ychsma cultures (around 200-1450 AD) built dozens of huacas; Spanish colonial Lima grew up around and on top of them.

question: The colonial city of Arequipa in southern Peru, founded in 1540 at the foot of three volcanoes, is built almost entirely of a single distinctive white-ish volcanic rock. The local cathedral, monasteries, and townhouses all share this material. What is this rock called?
answer: Sillar — a pale volcanic ignimbrite quarried from the deposits of Misti and Chachani above the city
choices: Sillar — a pale volcanic ignimbrite quarried from the deposits of Misti and Chachani above the city
Pumice — the bubbled, very light volcanic rock that is too soft for primary construction use
Travertine — a freshwater calcium-carbonate rock that does not form near volcanoes
Basalt — the dense dark volcanic rock most common across Peruvian highland archaeology
context: Sillar gives Arequipa its nickname 'La Ciudad Blanca' (the White City). The Monastery of Santa Catalina (founded 1579) is a near-complete walled town inside the city, all in sillar, only opened to outside visitors in 1970.

question: The seat of government of Bolivia sits in a long, deep canyon at 3,640 meters — the world's highest 'de facto' capital city. The city sprawls up the canyon walls, with poorer neighborhoods at higher elevations. Why is La Paz only the de facto and not the constitutional capital?
answer: The Bolivian constitution names Sucre as the constitutional capital, but the executive and legislature operate in La Paz
choices: The Bolivian constitution names Sucre as the constitutional capital, but the executive and legislature operate in La Paz
The Bolivian constitution names La Paz only as the seat of government, with Cochabamba as the constitutional capital
The Bolivian constitution is silent on the capital, but a 1899 civil war forced government move to La Paz
The Bolivian constitution makes Santa Cruz the capital, but its highland competition with La Paz has not been resolved
context: Sucre is the constitutional capital. La Paz became the de facto seat after the 1899 Federal War; the Supreme Court still sits in Sucre. The Mi Teleferico cable-car network climbs the canyon walls, the world's most extensive aerial-transit network.

question: The Bolivian city of Potosi, founded in 1545 at the foot of a single mountain, was for two centuries one of the largest and richest cities in the New World — its silver fuelled the Spanish empire and the global economy. Which mountain rises above the city?
answer: Cerro Rico ('Rich Mountain'), an extinct stratovolcano whose silver veins supplied roughly 60% of the world's silver between 1556 and 1783
choices: Cerro Rico ('Rich Mountain'), an extinct stratovolcano whose silver veins supplied roughly 60% of the world's silver between 1556 and 1783
Illimani, the snow-capped peak that dominates La Paz farther north in the Bolivian altiplano
Mount Sajama, the highest mountain in Bolivia, near the Chilean border on the southwestern altiplano
Tunari, the peak above Cochabamba in central Bolivia
context: The Spanish forced enslaved Africans and Indigenous Andeans into the mines under the mita labour system. Death tolls were enormous. Potosi's mountain is now hollowed out and slowly collapsing; small-scale silver mining still goes on inside its tunnels.

question: On the eastern coast of Brazil, the colonial city of Salvador was Brazil's first capital. Its Pelourinho historic district holds the densest concentration of 17th- and 18th-century colonial architecture in the Americas. Salvador has the largest population of African descent of any city outside Africa itself. What was its colonial economic foundation?
answer: Sugar plantations in the surrounding Recôncavo, worked by enslaved Africans transported through the port
choices: Sugar plantations in the surrounding Recôncavo, worked by enslaved Africans transported through the port
Gold and diamond mining in the inland Sertão, with miners passing through the port for inspection
Cattle ranching for tallow, leather, and dried beef exports back to Portugal under royal monopoly
Cocoa plantations established in the 16th century along the Bahian coast for European chocolate supply
context: Roughly 5 million enslaved Africans were brought to Brazil — about 40% of all Africans transported across the Atlantic. Salvador's Candomble religion preserved Yoruba and other West African traditions; the city's capoeira and Afro-Brazilian cuisine emerged here.

question: On the 700-meter peak of Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro stands a 30-meter art-deco statue with outstretched arms, finished in 1931 and visible from across the city. What does the statue depict, and who designed and built it?
answer: Christ the Redeemer — the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa designed the statue; the French sculptor Paul Landowski sculpted the head and hands
choices: Christ the Redeemer — the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa designed the statue; the French sculptor Paul Landowski sculpted the head and hands
Saint Sebastian (patron of Rio) — the Portuguese sculptor Aleijadinho designed it and Brazilian masons constructed it
Saint Anthony (patron of Lisbon) — a joint commission between Portuguese architects and Brazilian engineers
Saint Christopher (patron of travelers) — a German-Brazilian collaboration funded by 19th-century immigrants
context: The statue cost roughly $250,000 in 1931 dollars, funded largely by donations from Brazilian Catholics. It took five years to construct out of soapstone-clad reinforced concrete. Standing on the rim of the Tijuca National Park, it is now one of the most-photographed monuments on Earth.

question: In the dockside neighborhood of La Boca in Buenos Aires, Argentina, around the 1880s, a new music began among the immigrant longshoremen, sailors, and dock workers — a syncopated 2/4 dance for couples in close embrace, blending European, African, and Latin American sources. What is this dance?
answer: Tango — emerging in the brothels and tenements (conventillos) of La Boca and Montevideo before becoming a global ballroom dance
choices: Tango — emerging in the brothels and tenements (conventillos) of La Boca and Montevideo before becoming a global ballroom dance
Bossa nova — actually a Brazilian style emerging in Rio de Janeiro in the 1950s, decades later
Cumbia — a Colombian Caribbean dance emerging in the 1820s with a different rhythm and origins
Mambo — a Cuban style from Havana of the 1940s, much later than the Argentine tango
context: The bandoneon, a German invention shipped to Argentina in the late 19th century, became the tango's defining instrument. Carlos Gardel's 1935 plane-crash death in Medellin remains a touchstone of tango legend. UNESCO inscribed tango in 2009.

question: In the central Recoleta neighborhood of Buenos Aires lies a 14-acre walled cemetery whose alleys are lined with marble mausoleums of Argentina's elite families. The most-visited tomb belongs to a woman who never held elected office but whose embalmed body sat for decades in various continents before reaching her final resting place. Who is she?
answer: Eva Peron ('Evita'), the wife of Argentine president Juan Peron, who died of cancer in 1952 at age 33
choices: Eva Peron ('Evita'), the wife of Argentine president Juan Peron, who died of cancer in 1952 at age 33
Mercedes Sosa, the great Argentine folk singer who died in 2009
Victoria Ocampo, the Argentine literary patron and founder of Sur magazine
Lola Mora, the early-20th-century Argentine sculptor whose nudes scandalised Buenos Aires
context: Evita's body had a strange post-death journey: stolen by anti-Peronist generals after the 1955 coup, hidden in Italy, then reburied finally at Recoleta in 1976. Argentine families pay enormous prices for any free Recoleta plot.

question: Some 3,500 km off the coast of Chile in the southeastern Pacific lies a small triangular volcanic island. Hundreds of carved stone figures called moai — most about 4 meters tall, the largest never finished, 21 meters tall — stand on stone platforms (ahu) facing inward across the island. What name do the islanders use for their home?
answer: Rapa Nui, the Polynesian name; Easter Island is the European name from the day Roggeveen reached it in 1722
choices: Rapa Nui, the Polynesian name; Easter Island is the European name from the day Roggeveen reached it in 1722
Te Pito o Te Henua, only — Rapa Nui is the name of a different island in the southern Cooks
Mata Ki Te Rangi ('Eyes Looking at the Sky'), used in Spanish administration only
Isla de Pascua, the original Polynesian name later translated into Spanish by colonial administrators
context: Te Pito o Te Henua ('Navel of the World') is also a Rapa Nui name, but Rapa Nui is the standard. The island is the easternmost outpost of Polynesia; Polynesians settled it perhaps as early as 1000 AD. Ecological collapse — possibly tied to rat-driven palm loss — preceded the European contact.

question: Modern Mexico City sits on the bed of a vast lake system that the Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan was built on top of as an artificial island in the 14th century. Why was the Spanish-period city sinking, and why does it continue to subside today?
answer: It rests on soft volcanic clay sediments of the former lake bed, compressed by buildings and groundwater pumping
choices: It rests on soft volcanic clay sediments of the former lake bed, compressed by buildings and groundwater pumping
It rests on volcanic ash from Popocatepetl, which absorbs water and expands during the rainy season
It rests on a sinkhole-prone limestone aquifer that periodically collapses beneath neighborhoods
It rests on a series of overlapping geological faults that allow gradual northward slide of the city floor
context: The Cathedral and Palacio Nacional lean visibly. Mexico City sinks roughly 50 cm per year in worst-affected zones — the most severe urban subsidence rate in the world. The Spanish drained the lake after 1521; Aztec chinampa agriculture survives only in Xochimilco.

question: About 50 km northeast of Mexico City lies an enormous ancient city — abandoned long before the Aztecs arrived. Its central axis, called the Avenue of the Dead, runs for 2.5 km between massive temple-pyramids. The city's actual name is unknown; the Aztecs gave it its current name. What does 'Teotihuacan' mean in Nahuatl?
answer: 'The Place Where the Gods Were Born' or 'Where People Become Gods'
choices: 'The Place Where the Gods Were Born' or 'Where People Become Gods'
'The Place of Eternal Springs' — a reference to its abundance of fresh water
'The City of the Sun' — a reference to its strict east-west orientation
'The Lost City' — the Aztec recognition that they did not know its original name
context: Teotihuacan flourished from roughly 100 BC to 550 AD and was probably the largest city in the Americas at its peak (perhaps 125,000 inhabitants). Its founders' identity remains unknown. The two main pyramids — of the Sun and the Moon — define the Avenue of the Dead.

question: On the Yucatan peninsula of Mexico stands one of the most famous Mayan-Toltec sites: a complex centred on a perfectly proportioned step-pyramid called El Castillo or the Temple of Kukulkan. Twice a year, at the equinoxes, a particular optical effect appears on the pyramid's stairway. What appears?
answer: The shadow of the corner forms a series of triangles that look like a serpent descending the north stairway
choices: The shadow of the corner forms a series of triangles that look like a serpent descending the north stairway
The pyramid casts a perfect circular shadow exactly matching the diameter of the nearby cenote
The pyramid's apex temple lights up red as a precise alignment of windows admits sunset light
The four corners of the pyramid each cast a separate shadow forming the points of a cross
context: The serpent is Kukulkan, the Mayan name for Quetzalcoatl. The pyramid's 365 steps (91 per side x 4, plus the platform) encode the solar year. Chichen Itza was inscribed by UNESCO in 1988 and is now one of the most-visited sites in Mexico.

question: On the Caribbean coast of Mexico's Yucatan peninsula sits the only known major Mayan walled city on the coast — built around 1200 AD as a Mayan trading port, with its main temple sitting on a 12-meter cliff over a turquoise sea below. What was the city's likely original name?
answer: Zama, meaning 'place of the dawn' in Yucatec Mayan — 'Tulum' (meaning 'wall') is a later term
choices: Zama, meaning 'place of the dawn' in Yucatec Mayan — 'Tulum' (meaning 'wall') is a later term
Xel-Ha, a related word meaning 'where the water is born,' the original name of the Mayan port
Bacalar, the freshwater lagoon city of the seven colours, located inland from the Caribbean coast
Coba, the inland Mayan city connected to Tulum by a sacbe (white road) running through jungle
context: Tulum was probably called Zama in its working period. Its coastal location is dramatic — the temple platform faces sunrise across the Caribbean. Coba is the inland sister site; sacbeob (Mayan paved roads) connected major sites across the peninsula.

question: In 1883, a steel-cable suspension bridge opened between Manhattan and Brooklyn — at 486 meters main-span the longest suspension bridge in the world, the first to use steel cables. Which family of engineers designed and supervised the bridge?
answer: John A. Roebling started it; his son Washington Roebling oversaw construction; Washington's wife Emily Warren Roebling completed it
choices: John A. Roebling started it; his son Washington Roebling oversaw construction; Washington's wife Emily Warren Roebling completed it
Gustave Eiffel led the design while his son-in-law Adolphe Salles supervised the New York site
James Eads designed it after completing his famous Mississippi bridge at St. Louis
Squire Whipple designed it as the culmination of his American truss-bridge career
context: John Roebling died from injuries before construction began. Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease (the bends) overseeing underwater foundation work and was paralysed; his wife Emily took over operational oversight and is credited as the bridge's effective chief engineer in its final decade.

question: Inside Grand Central Terminal in Manhattan, a vast painted barrel-vault ceiling shows constellations and the zodiac in green-and-gold leaf. The ceiling has one famous oddity, discovered after the painting's completion in 1913. What is the oddity?
answer: The constellations are painted backwards (mirror-reversed) — possibly intentional, possibly an error
choices: The constellations are painted backwards (mirror-reversed) — possibly intentional, possibly an error
Three of the constellations were painted with their stars rearranged in patterns invented by the painter
The painted zodiac shows fourteen signs rather than the twelve of traditional Western astrology
The colours of the ceiling shift over time because of a rare temperature-sensitive copper pigment
context: The reversal may have been intentional ('as God sees the sky from above'), an artistic flourish, or a mistake. A small rectangle of original pre-1998-restoration ceiling is left visible in the northwest corner to show the smoke-damaged colour.

question: In the middle of Manhattan island, between roughly 59th and 110th Streets, stretches a rectangular park 4 km long by 800 meters wide. Its designers shaped it carefully in the 1850s with hills, lakes, meadows, and rocky outcrops to look like wild scenery. Who were the lead designers?
answer: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who won an 1858 design competition with their 'Greensward Plan'
choices: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who won an 1858 design competition with their 'Greensward Plan'
Daniel Burnham, the Chicago architect who later designed the 1893 World's Fair in his hometown
Frank Lloyd Wright, the leading American architect of the early 20th century
Andrew Jackson Downing, who actually died before any New York park work began in 1852
context: Olmsted went on to design Brooklyn's Prospect Park, Boston's Emerald Necklace, and dozens of other major American parks. Downing championed the idea of a major New York park but died in 1852 before its construction; his ideas shaped the project.

question: The world's first steel-framed skyscraper — the 10-story Home Insurance Building — was completed in a major American city in 1885. What city was it, and what made the building possible?
answer: Chicago, where Major William Le Baron Jenney pioneered a steel-frame structure carrying the weight independently of the masonry walls
choices: Chicago, where Major William Le Baron Jenney pioneered a steel-frame structure carrying the weight independently of the masonry walls
New York, where Daniel Burnham's Flatiron Building used the same steel-frame technique a generation later
Pittsburgh, where Andrew Carnegie's local steel mills supplied the first structural-steel I-beams for the project
Boston, where the John Hancock Tower used the same technique three-quarters of a century later still
context: Pre-1885 'tall' buildings depended on thick load-bearing brick walls that grew prohibitively thick above 8 stories. Steel framing let buildings rise much higher. The Home Insurance Building stood until 1931; the Chicago school of architecture (Sullivan, Adler, Burnham) reshaped American cities.

question: Around 1900, in the dance halls, brothels, and street parades of an American Gulf Coast city, a new music began to coalesce — improvisational, syncopated, blue-tinted, blending European wind instruments with African rhythmic sensibility. What city, and what neighborhood was its hot zone?
answer: New Orleans, in the Storyville district and Black neighborhoods like Treme
choices: New Orleans, in the Storyville district and Black neighborhoods like Treme
Memphis, on Beale Street near the Mississippi steamboat docks
Kansas City, in the Eighteenth and Vine entertainment district
Chicago, on the South Side along State and Calumet Streets
context: Memphis, Kansas City, and Chicago all became major jazz centres later, but New Orleans is the consensus birthplace. Buddy Bolden, Jelly Roll Morton, and Louis Armstrong all came out of New Orleans. The 1917 closing of Storyville sent jazz musicians up the Mississippi toward Memphis, St. Louis, and Chicago.

question: The Golden Gate Bridge across the entrance to San Francisco Bay, completed in 1937, is famously painted in a particular reddish-orange colour rather than the gold or grey one might assume from its name. What is this colour officially called, and why?
answer: 'International Orange,' chosen by chief architect Irving Morrow because it blends with the bridge's coastal setting and is visible in fog
choices: 'International Orange,' chosen by chief architect Irving Morrow because it blends with the bridge's coastal setting and is visible in fog
'Sealing-Wax Red,' chosen to match the original Navy's red paint stocks available at the construction site
'Sunset Vermillion,' chosen to match the actual sunset hue over the Pacific west of the bridge
'California Cinnabar,' chosen to match the rust colour of natural deposits in the Marin headlands
context: Morrow's choice has become iconic. The Navy had wanted black and yellow stripes, and the Army Air Corps had suggested red and white candy stripes for aerial visibility; Morrow argued the orange complemented the brown hills and was lost only in the heaviest fog.

question: San Francisco operates a cable-car system originally laid out in the 1870s — wooden trams that grip a constantly moving underground steel cable to climb the city's steep hills. Most cities long ago replaced their cable cars with electric streetcars. San Francisco's system has a particular distinction. What is it?
answer: It is the only manually operated cable car system still operating anywhere in the world
choices: It is the only manually operated cable car system still operating anywhere in the world
It is the longest cable car system, with over 200 km of operating track
It is the oldest cable-driven public transit, with continuous service since the 1820s
It is the fastest cable car system in the world, with top speeds of 60 km/h
context: Andrew Smith Hallidie opened the first San Francisco cable car line in 1873. Citizen activists led by Friedel Klussmann saved the system from closure in 1947; the cable cars are a designated National Historic Landmark.

question: On the border between Brazil and Argentina, in a tropical rainforest, the Iguazu river plunges over a wide basalt escarpment in a series of 275 separate cataracts spread along 2.7 km. The largest single drop is a horseshoe-shaped chasm that swallows roughly half the river's flow. What is this central horseshoe called in Portuguese and Spanish?
answer: Garganta do Diabo (Portuguese) / Garganta del Diablo (Spanish) — 'the Devil's Throat'
choices: Garganta do Diabo (Portuguese) / Garganta del Diablo (Spanish) — 'the Devil's Throat'
Cataracta Grande (Portuguese) / Catarata Mayor (Spanish) — 'the Great Cataract'
Garganta da Onca (Portuguese) / Garganta del Jaguar (Spanish) — 'the Jaguar's Throat'
Cachoeira da Aurora (Portuguese) / Catarata de la Aurora (Spanish) — 'the Falls of the Dawn'
context: Iguazu is wider than Victoria Falls and taller than Niagara; on first sight Eleanor Roosevelt is said to have remarked 'Poor Niagara.' The Devil's Throat alone drops 82 meters; its mist sometimes rises hundreds of meters above the surrounding jungle.

question: Johannesburg is the largest South African city — and unusually for a major world city, it is not built on a coast, river, or harbour. What put a city there?
answer: The 1886 discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef, the largest gold field ever found, beneath the empty grasslands of the high veld
choices: The 1886 discovery of the Witwatersrand gold reef, the largest gold field ever found, beneath the empty grasslands of the high veld
The 1820 settlement of British colonists fleeing the eastern Cape, planted at a strategic high-veld site
The 1854 founding by Boer voortrekkers seeking refuge between two coastal British colonies
The 1899 British military fortress built during the Second Boer War, which became a refugee settlement
context: Within decades of 1886 Johannesburg ballooned from empty veld to a major industrial city. Witwatersrand ore has produced roughly 40% of all gold ever mined. The city's deep gold mines are now mostly closed; mining moved north and far underground.

question: The Nigerian city of Lagos is the largest urban agglomeration in sub-Saharan Africa, with a population estimated above 20 million. The historic core sits on islands and peninsulas in a coastal lagoon system. Under what circumstances did Lagos cease being Nigeria's capital?
answer: The capital moved to a newly built planned city in central Nigeria, Abuja, in 1991
choices: The capital moved to a newly built planned city in central Nigeria, Abuja, in 1991
The capital moved to Ibadan (the historic Yoruba inland city) in 1976 after a constitutional reform
The capital moved to Kano (the northern Hausa-Fulani trading city) in 1985 as part of national balance
The capital moved to Port Harcourt (the southern oil-region city) in 1999 after the return to democracy
context: Abuja was built on a previously empty site in the Federal Capital Territory for political-geographic balance among Nigeria's regions. Lagos State remains by far the country's economic engine despite no longer holding the capital.

question: The Ethiopian capital, founded in 1886 by Empress Taitu Betul and her husband Menelik II, sits at 2,400 meters in the highlands of central Ethiopia — making it Africa's highest national capital and the third-highest in the world. The city hosts the permanent headquarters of a major international body. Which body?
answer: The African Union, headquartered in Addis Ababa since the body's founding in 2002 (and previously the OAU since 1963)
choices: The African Union, headquartered in Addis Ababa since the body's founding in 2002 (and previously the OAU since 1963)
The Arab League, headquartered in Cairo since 1945 with a small Addis liaison office
The UN's economic commission for Asia (ESCAP), headquartered farther east in Bangkok
The International Court of Justice, headquartered in The Hague rather than in Africa
context: Ethiopia was the only African state never colonised (with the brief exception of Italian occupation, 1936-1941), giving Addis Ababa Pan-African symbolic weight. The AU complex was a 2012 gift from China, part of its expanded relationship with the continent.

question: Off the coast of Senegal, opposite the modern capital of Dakar, lies a small island about 900 meters long with a famous pink-stone 'House of Slaves' (Maison des Esclaves) and its 'Door of No Return' opening directly onto the Atlantic. What is this island called?
answer: Goree Island, used by European traders as a trading post from the 15th to 19th centuries
choices: Goree Island, used by European traders as a trading post from the 15th to 19th centuries
Bunce Island, a different West African slave-trade island in Sierra Leone with English ruins
Elmina Island, the Portuguese-built fortress on the Gold Coast in modern Ghana
Cape Coast Island, also in Ghana, another major Atlantic slave-trading fortress
context: Some historians dispute the literal volume of slave embarkations from Goree itself (it was perhaps a smaller node than Elmina or Bunce), but the island's symbolic role is enormous. UNESCO inscribed it in 1978 and three U.S. presidents have visited in person.

question: On Bennelong Point on Sydney Harbour, Australia, stand the white-shelled vaults of an opera house finished in 1973 after fourteen years of difficult construction. Its iconic billowing concrete 'sails' were the work of a young Danish architect who won the 1957 design competition. Who was he?
answer: Jorn Utzon, who resigned from the project in 1966 over cost disputes and never returned to see it finished
choices: Jorn Utzon, who resigned from the project in 1966 over cost disputes and never returned to see it finished
Eero Saarinen, the Finnish-American architect of the TWA Terminal in New York in the same era
Le Corbusier, the Swiss-French architect of contemporary projects in Marseille and Chandigarh
Frank Lloyd Wright, who actually died in 1959 before completion of the Sydney design competition
context: Utzon's resignation became one of the great architectural tragedies of the 20th century. He never visited the finished building. A 1999 reconciliation appointed Utzon as design consultant for renovations; his son Jan Utzon carried out interior reworking after Utzon's death in 2008.

question: In the centre of the Australian continent, in arid red-earth country, rises a single enormous sandstone monolith — 348 meters tall, 9.4 km in circumference, and most of its bulk still hidden underground. The local Anangu Aboriginal people regard it as sacred. What is it called, and what does it physically consist of?
answer: Uluru — a single block of arkose sandstone that has weathered out as the surrounding sediments eroded away
choices: Uluru — a single block of arkose sandstone that has weathered out as the surrounding sediments eroded away
Mount Augustus — a single block of granite that crystallised from a magma chamber in the Pilbara
Wave Rock — a curving 14-meter sandstone wall in the Western Australian wheatbelt
The Olgas (Kata Tjuta) — a separate cluster of dome-shaped conglomerate rocks 30 km west of Uluru
context: Mount Augustus and Kata Tjuta both exist; Mount Augustus claims to be larger than Uluru. Climbing Uluru was permanently banned from October 2019 out of respect for the Anangu. Sunrise and sunset light dramatically shifts the rock's colour.

question: Off Australia's northeastern coast stretches the world's largest reef system — about 2,300 km long, made of roughly 3,000 individual reefs and 900 islands. It can be seen from space and is the largest single structure built by living organisms. What organisms built it?
answer: Coral polyps, tiny anemone-like animals secreting calcium carbonate skeletons that accumulate over millennia
choices: Coral polyps, tiny anemone-like animals secreting calcium carbonate skeletons that accumulate over millennia
Pearl oysters, whose shells build up into reef-like aggregations along the coast over thousands of years
Coralline algae, which secrete calcium carbonate independently of any animal contribution
Sponges, simple multicellular animals whose silica spicules slowly bind sediment into reef rock
context: Coralline algae and sponges contribute, but reef-building corals (Scleractinia) are the primary builders. The Great Barrier Reef has lost roughly half its coral cover since 1985 to bleaching, crown-of-thorns starfish, and cyclone damage; conservation pressure intensifies.

question: The largest New Zealand city is built across a low isthmus between two harbours, and across more than 50 separate small volcanoes whose cones and craters now dot the city — many of them prominent landmarks like Mount Eden and One Tree Hill. What kind of volcanic field is this?
answer: A monogenetic volcanic field — each cone is a single short-lived volcano that erupted once and then went extinct
choices: A monogenetic volcanic field — each cone is a single short-lived volcano that erupted once and then went extinct
A composite-stratovolcano field — the city sits inside the eroded caldera of a single ancient large volcano
A shield-volcano field — like Hawaii, the cones formed from successive lava effusions on flat ground
A caldera field — multiple overlapping calderas have collapsed and refilled over millennia
context: The youngest cone in the Auckland Volcanic Field is Rangitoto, just offshore — only about 600 years old. The whole field remains active (geologically); the next eruption will almost certainly come from a new vent rather than from an existing cone.

question: Easter Island lies 2,000 km from its nearest inhabited neighbor (Pitcairn) and 3,500 km from the South American coast. Yet Polynesians settled it around 1000 AD using only ocean-going canoes and wayfinding skills. What was their navigational method?
answer: Stars, ocean swells, bird flight, and cloud patterns — passed down through specialist navigator castes for generations
choices: Stars, ocean swells, bird flight, and cloud patterns — passed down through specialist navigator castes for generations
Magnetic compasses adapted from Chinese trading partners reaching the South Pacific in the 9th century
Sea charts inscribed on pandanus leaves, marking depth and current along major Pacific crossings
Astrolabes constructed from coconut shell and bone, adapted from medieval Arab navigational tools
context: Polynesian wayfinding has been revived in the late 20th century — the Hawaiian voyaging canoe Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 using only traditional methods, and again in 2014-2017 around the entire world.

question: On New Zealand's North Island, around the town of Rotorua, the ground steams and bubbles — boiling mud pools, sulfur fumaroles, periodic geysers. The Te Arawa Maori people built villages on top of this thermal landscape, sometimes cooking food in geothermal pools. What was the most famous lost natural wonder of this region?
answer: The Pink and White Terraces — silica-deposit travertine terraces on Lake Rotomahana, destroyed in the 1886 eruption of Mount Tarawera
choices: The Pink and White Terraces — silica-deposit travertine terraces on Lake Rotomahana, destroyed in the 1886 eruption of Mount Tarawera
The Great Geyser — a 70-meter regular geyser at Whakarewarewa that stopped erupting after a 1923 earthquake
The Boiling River — a stretch of the Waikato River that boiled at the surface until 1950s hydroelectric development
The Burning Mountain — a sulfur-veined hill that smouldered visibly for centuries before going out in the 1880s
context: The Pink and White Terraces had been the most-visited tourist destination of pre-1886 New Zealand. The 1886 Tarawera eruption killed roughly 120 people and buried them under ash; in 2017 sonar imagery suggested fragments of the terraces may still exist on the lake bed.

question: On the north bank of the Douro river in northern Portugal, the city of Porto descends steeply from the upper town to the riverside Ribeira quarter — a UNESCO-listed warren of narrow streets and 18th-century houses leaning together. Just across the river is the city of Vila Nova de Gaia. Why is this geographic split historically important?
answer: Port wine ages and is shipped from cellars in Gaia, while Porto on the opposite bank is where merchants and shippers lived
choices: Port wine ages and is shipped from cellars in Gaia, while Porto on the opposite bank is where merchants and shippers lived
Porto's law forbade industrial activity inside the medieval walls, so all warehousing was forced across the river to Gaia
The Douro was the historical border between two medieval kingdoms, with Porto in Castille and Gaia in Portugal
Porto was Catholic and Gaia was Protestant during the Reformation, so the two banks developed independently
context: Until 1986 it was illegal to ship Port wine into Porto without first aging it in Gaia. The barcos rabelos that once carried the wine downriver now sit moored along the Ribeira for tourists.

question: Iguazu Falls thunders along the Brazil-Argentina border in a tropical rainforest. The Iguazu river drops over a wide volcanic escarpment in 275 separate cataracts spread along 2.7 kilometres of cliff. The greatest single drop is a horseshoe-shaped gorge swallowing roughly half the river's flow. Iguazu's average flow puts it in what global rank for waterfall water volume?
answer: Among the largest in the world, generally ranking ahead of Niagara and behind Victoria Falls in average flow
choices: Among the largest in the world, generally ranking ahead of Niagara and behind Victoria Falls in average flow
The largest by volume, surpassing Victoria Falls by roughly threefold during the rainy season
Significantly below the world top ten, ranking after Khone Falls and several Norwegian rivers
In the top hundred only, with most of its visual size coming from its width rather than its actual flow
context: Iguazu's average flow is around 1,750 m^3/s; the much smaller Khone Falls in Laos has higher peak flow but Iguazu is a steady high-volume wonder. Victoria Falls has higher water volume at peak; Niagara is considerably smaller.

question: The Niagara River drops 51 meters between Lakes Erie and Ontario in a wide curtain split by Goat Island into two main falls — the American Falls on the U.S. side and the larger Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side. Roughly what fraction of the river's flow goes over the Canadian Horseshoe?
answer: About 90 percent — the Horseshoe is much deeper and curved, capturing the river's main channel
choices: About 90 percent — the Horseshoe is much deeper and curved, capturing the river's main channel
About 60 percent — the two falls are roughly equal in flow with a slight Canadian majority
About 50 percent — the river splits evenly around Goat Island into the two falls
About 25 percent — most of the river's water goes over the wider American Falls, leaving the Horseshoe quieter
context: Hydroelectric diversion under treaty between the U.S. and Canada drastically reduces the river's flow at night and in winter to power both nations' grids. The Horseshoe recedes (retreats upstream) about 1 meter every 10 years.

question: On the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, the Zambezi river drops 108 meters over a long basalt cliff in a wide curtain — perhaps the largest single sheet of falling water on Earth at high flow. The local Lozi name for the falls translates as 'the smoke that thunders.' What is the local name?
answer: Mosi-oa-Tunya — visible mist rises hundreds of meters above the falls, audible from many kilometres away
choices: Mosi-oa-Tunya — visible mist rises hundreds of meters above the falls, audible from many kilometres away
Shongwe — the historical Tonga name meaning 'the place of the rainbow'
Aman'a Mthonga — a Ndebele name meaning 'water of the great rope'
Sungwe — an early Portuguese trader's name still used along the upper Zambezi
context: David Livingstone named the falls for Queen Victoria in 1855; UNESCO uses both names. The full curtain spans 1.7 km. The falls drop into a series of zig-zag gorges, evidence of the falls' progressive upstream retreat through basalt joints.

question: Deep in the Canaima rainforest of southeastern Venezuela, water plunges over the edge of a flat-topped sandstone mesa for 979 meters in a single uninterrupted drop — the tallest waterfall in the world. The cataract is so high that much of the water evaporates into mist before reaching the bottom. What is the falls called, and from which mesa does it drop?
answer: Angel Falls, dropping from Auyan-tepui, named for the American pilot Jimmie Angel who landed atop the mesa in 1937
choices: Angel Falls, dropping from Auyan-tepui, named for the American pilot Jimmie Angel who landed atop the mesa in 1937
Kaieteur Falls, dropping from Kukenan-tepui, named for the indigenous Pemon chief Kaie
Iguazu Falls, dropping from a basalt plateau, named after the Tupi-Guarani word for 'big water'
Wallaman Falls, dropping from the Atherton Tableland, named for the local Australian Aboriginal language
context: Auyan-tepui means 'Devil's Mountain' in the Pemon language. The tepuis (table mountains) of the Guiana Highlands are flat-topped Precambrian sandstone, among the oldest exposed rock formations on Earth.

question: In the Potaro river of central Guyana, water drops 226 meters in a single uninterrupted plunge — five times higher than Niagara, dropping nearly four times the height of Iguazu's main fall. The falls are wide (about 113 meters across) and high-volume. What is this waterfall called?
answer: Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's most powerful single-drop falls by combined height and flow
choices: Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's most powerful single-drop falls by combined height and flow
Angel Falls, the tallest waterfall in the world, located in southeastern Venezuela
Tugela Falls, the second-tallest waterfall in the world, located in South Africa's Drakensberg
Yumbilla Falls, a high but narrow Andean cascade in northern Peru
context: Kaieteur sits inside a national park with very little development; visitors arrive by small plane. The falls are home to a unique golden frog, found only in the bromeliads growing in the perpetual mist of the gorge.

question: On the Hvita river in southwestern Iceland, glacial meltwater drops in two stepped cascades into a deep canyon — a U-shaped first step, then a turn through 90 degrees into a deeper drop. Mist rising from the canyon often hangs golden in afternoon sun. What is the falls called?
answer: Gullfoss ('the Golden Falls'), Iceland's most famous waterfall on the popular tourist route called the Golden Circle
choices: Gullfoss ('the Golden Falls'), Iceland's most famous waterfall on the popular tourist route called the Golden Circle
Dettifoss ('the Tumbling Falls'), Europe's most powerful waterfall on the Jokulsa a Fjollum river
Skogafoss ('the Forest Falls'), a sheer-curtain waterfall on the south coast of Iceland
Seljalandsfoss ('the Sea-Edge Falls'), a curtain waterfall on the south coast that visitors can walk behind
context: Gullfoss was nearly converted into a hydroelectric project in the early 20th century; the daughter of the local farmer who owned the falls, Sigridur Tomasdottir, walked to Reykjavik repeatedly to protest. The state purchased and protected the falls in 1979.

question: In central Croatia, a series of 16 turquoise lakes connected by cascading travertine terraces — natural stone dams made of calcium carbonate built by mosses and microbes — descend through a forested valley. The colour of the water shifts from green-blue to grey with the seasons. What is this national park called?
answer: Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia's oldest national park (1949) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
choices: Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia's oldest national park (1949) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Krka National Park, also a Croatian travertine system but located in central Dalmatia
Una National Park, located across the Bosnian border in the Una river valley
Velebit Mountain National Park, the long karstic ridge running parallel to the Croatian coastline
context: Travertine forms at Plitvice when calcium-saturated water deposits onto plant material and microbial mats; the lake dams are still growing. The park is one of Croatia's most-visited natural sites and a remarkable example of active carbonate landscape.

question: Deep in the Grand Canyon of Arizona, on land belonging to the Havasupai Tribe, water plunges over orange sandstone into a series of stunning turquoise pools. The water's deep blue-green colour comes from dissolved minerals. What is the mineral?
answer: Calcium carbonate, dissolved from limestone upstream and giving the water its characteristic Caribbean colour
choices: Calcium carbonate, dissolved from limestone upstream and giving the water its characteristic Caribbean colour
Copper sulfate, leached from nearby copper-mining deposits in the canyon walls
Iron oxide, picked up from the surrounding red rocks giving the water its slightly metallic colour
Silica from volcanic ash deposits in the headwaters that scatter blue light
context: Calcium carbonate also deposits on the streambed as travertine, making the pools' surface slightly shelf-like. Havasu Creek joins the Colorado River deep in the Grand Canyon; the Havasupai Reservation manages tourism on this remote stretch.

question: The Nile is the world's longest river — between 6,650 and 6,853 km depending on the source measured — and is unusual among major rivers for the direction it flows. From its sources in the African highlands, the Nile flows in which direction?
answer: Northward, from the highlands of east Africa across the Sahara to the Mediterranean Sea
choices: Northward, from the highlands of east Africa across the Sahara to the Mediterranean Sea
Eastward, from central African headwaters to the Indian Ocean near Mogadishu
Southward, from Ethiopian highlands to a large delta on the Mozambique coastline
Westward, from the Sudd marshes across the Sahel to a delta on the Atlantic Ocean
context: The Nile contradicted European intuition (later rivers tend to flow toward equator-warm air) — northern explorers confused even Roman geographers. The Amazon-vs-Nile longest-river dispute continues: claims based on extended Andean tributaries put the Amazon slightly ahead.

question: At the Sudanese capital of Khartoum, two major tributaries of the Nile meet to form the main Nile that flows north through Egypt. The two are named for the colour of their waters at certain seasons. What are they?
answer: The White Nile (from East Africa via Uganda and South Sudan) and the Blue Nile (from the Ethiopian highlands)
choices: The White Nile (from East Africa via Uganda and South Sudan) and the Blue Nile (from the Ethiopian highlands)
The Eastern Nile (from Eritrea) and the Western Nile (from Chad), each contributing roughly half
The Upper Nile (from Lake Victoria) and the Lower Nile (from the Sudd wetlands), separated at the cataracts
The Sobat (from Ethiopia) and the Bahr el Ghazal (from Sudan), the two principal pre-Khartoum tributaries
